Left alone it would have told an operator to perform a step that is now automatic, and implied the release stamping was still unreliable. Rewritten to keep the image-retention half (still manual) and record that the build arg is declarative now, with the docker-compose.yml caveat. That is the same-commit vault rule catching a drift I introduced. THE REAL ADDITION IS AC2's STRUCTURAL PREVENTION for claim (1). The row currently protects itself with the PROSE 'Do not hardcode a version here' — and prose is not enforcement, which is the recurring lesson of this whole session. New guard in cron-registry-drift_test.ts fails the build if the migrations row re-acquires an assertion of the form 'latest = 00123'. It deliberately allows a version cited while EXPLAINING history ('this row previously read latest = 00132'), because banning digits outright would delete the very sentence that stops someone re-adding the number. WORTH RECORDING WHY 'ask the system' BEATS 'generate the line', since AC2 proposed generating it: a generated value would be the REPO's max migration, which is NOT what PROD has applied — a distinction this repo learned the hard way when /health/ready reported an applied version with no corresponding file in the tree (the phantom 00479, see PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md). Generating would have produced a confident, wrong number. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED, AND MY FIRST ATTEMPT WAS WRONG IN AN INSTRUCTIVE WAY: my sabotage regex used [^|]* and the row contains ESCAPED pipes, so it replaced only a prefix and left the explanatory clause intact — the guard then correctly stayed silent and I nearly read that as the guard failing. Replaced the whole row properly; it then fails with the CONFIRMING-direction message. That is the fifth time this session a shell-driven edit did something other than what it printed. STILL OPEN: (3) rollback validation has never been executed once and needs a staging deploy — it is a LAUNCH-BLOCKER and cannot be closed from a checkout; (4) VITE_POSTHOG_KEY is empty so analytics.ts skips posthog.init entirely, and whether PostHog is intended for launch is a product decision — set the key or remove the claim, but do not leave a dark integration that reads as wired.

userStories.title: Correlated fail-open: one DB blip removes per-user rate limiting AND the AI spend kill-switch together
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want cost controls that do not all fail at once. middleware/rate-limit.ts:185 defaults failClosed to false and :264-267 logs 'allowing request (fail-open)' on a store error. The grading endpoint does not opt in — main.ts:821 rateLimiter(... 'grade') has no failClosed, unlike main.ts:792/:795/:800 which do. Separately lib/ai-budget-gate.ts:9-12 is FAIL-OPEN on error and :36-41 caches an EMPTY killed-set for the TTL on failure. Both controls read the same Postgres, so they share a failure domain: during a Postgres degradation, per-user grading rate limits and the hard USD kill-switch disappear SIMULTANEOUSLY while Anthropic stays up and billable.
acceptanceCriteria: Add failClosed: true to the grade and flipdesk-ai limiters, or make ai-budget-gate fail CLOSED specifically for action=kill budgets.
Ensure the two controls do not share a single failure domain, or accept the correlation explicitly and document the residual exposure in dollars.
Note the argument is the CORRELATION, not fail-open as a policy — fail-open per-control is a deliberate and defensible choice; two failing together is what turns a degradation into an unbounded bill.
userStories.notes: [P2][Cost/Reliability] Found 2026-07-18 by the operational-readiness deep dive. Mitigating and worth stating: the ai-limiter.ts global semaphore and daily call ceiling SURVIVE a DB outage and are the real backstop — the audit rated the layered cost control correct overall. But the daily ceiling is a blunt global, not a per-tenant guard, so a single abusive or looping tenant can consume it during the window. | 2026-07-18 PARTIALLY FIXED (agent loop). Added failClosed: true to BOTH AI-spend limiters — /api/grade/* (main.ts, the DB-backed rate_limit_grade_per_min resolver) and /api/flipdesk/ai/*. Rationale recorded at both call sites: each control failing open is defensible in isolation, and I did not change that policy generally; what is not defensible is that this limiter and lib/ai-budget-gate.ts read the SAME Postgres, so a single degradation removed per-user grading limits and the hard USD kill-switch simultaneously while Anthropic stayed up and billable. Closing the two most expensive surfaces breaks the correlation where it costs the most: during a store outage a caller now gets a 429 and retries instead of an uncapped fan-out to the vision API. Verified: deno check clean, 4148 edge tests pass. STILL OPEN: AC2 — ai-budget-gate itself remains fail-open for action=kill budgets, and the deeper question of whether these two controls should share a failure domain at all is unresolved. Also unchanged and worth remembering: the ai-limiter.ts global semaphore and daily call ceiling SURVIVE a DB outage and are the real backstop, but the daily ceiling is a blunt global, so one looping tenant can still consume it inside the window. | 2026-07-19 AC2 DONE — story complete. FIRST, A STALE-NOTE CORRECTION: the prior pass recorded 'STILL OPEN: ai-budget-gate itself remains fail-open for action=kill budgets'. That is no longer true and I checked the TREE rather than trusting the note — ai-budget-gate.ts already RETAINS the last known kill set on a read error (lastKnownKilled), with 5 tests including the retention and recovery cases. The sharper framing of that original bug is worth keeping: it did not merely fail open, it cached an EMPTY set for the TTL, which ACTIVELY ERASED a known breach — a feature whose hard USD ceiling had already been hit resumed spending for 30s per failed read, for as long as the outage lasted. An error can no longer un-kill anything. WHAT I ACTUALLY ADDED: an audit of which AI-SPENDING surfaces still failed open, which nobody had enumerated. Found three and closed them — /api/flipdesk/scout/* (the highest fan-out request on the platform after grading: it grades N candidates per scan, which is exactly why its cap is 6/min, so leaving that cap fail-open removed the bound on the most expensive surface), /api/support/assistant/* (an LLM route), and /api/flipdesk/autolister/* WRITES (a batch enqueue kicks off per-item generateListing calls, so it spends AI even though the request itself is cheap). VERIFIED /api/grade/snap needs no change: it is covered transitively, because Hono runs the /api/grade/* group limiter on it too and that one is failClosed — worth recording, since the snap limiter reads as an unprotected AI path if you only look at its own options object. DELIBERATE ASYMMETRY, which is the judgement here: the autolister READ poll stays fail-open. It buys no tokens, and 429ing a status poll during a blip would break the queue view for a batch already running and already paid for. Same for /product and /measure, which are eBay Browse and CPU-only image work with no model call. Close what SPENDS, not what reads — closing a read path buys no safety and costs availability. AC2's second half ('accept the correlation explicitly and document the residual exposure IN DOLLARS') is answered in a new vault note, vault/10-ops/ai-spend-failure-domain.md: worst case ~$850 for a full day of TOTAL Postgres outage at one replica, derived from AI_GLOBAL_DAILY_CALL_CEILING (50,000/day) x ~$0.017/call, scaling LINEARLY with replica count because ai-limiter's degraded fallback counter is per-process. The note states plainly that $0.017 is an ESTIMATE from list pricing and typical token counts, NOT a measurement, and gives the exact ai_usage query to replace it — the bound is only as good as that input and it is the one nobody has measured. Also records WHY the correlation is accepted rather than eliminated: a separate limiter store (Redis/process-local) would remove the shared failure domain outright, but adds an infra dependency and a consistency problem to solve a bill already bounded at roughly a day's ceiling. Revisit if replica count or the ceiling rises. Verified: edge 4237 passed, deno check + lint clean, vault-lint clean (which also caught that my constants.ts edit had drifted grading-scale-and-weights.md — re-read, weights unchanged, reviewed bumped).

userStories.title: 23 route groups touching multi-tenant tables have no tenant-isolation test case; /api/account is the priority
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want the US-268 per-route test rule to actually hold. tenant-isolation_test.ts is strong — 118 cases making real HTTP foreign-tenant probes — but these mounts have ZERO coverage: /api/account (reaches submissions, grade_reports, inventory_items, listings, sales, item_photos, sources — it both exports AND deletes), /api/flipdesk/images, /api/flipdesk/equity, /api/flipdesk/scout, /api/flipdesk/shopify, /api/flipdesk/depop, /api/flipdesk/google, /api/guarantee, /api/drip, /api/webhooks, plus 13 /api/admin/* groups.
acceptanceCriteria: Add cases for the ordinary seller routes first: /api/account (highest — seven multi-tenant tables), then /api/flipdesk/images and /api/flipdesk/equity.
Treat the /api/admin/* groups as lower priority and document why: adminAuthMiddleware covers them at main.ts:730-731, so they are authorization-gated by design rather than tenant-gated.

ALSO from the same audit — invert the auth allowlist for /api/flipdesk/ebay. main.ts:401-543 enumerates ~90 individual paths while other modules use a /* wildcard. All 108 currently-unmatched paths were hand-verified as legitimately public or self-authenticating (OAuth callbacks, requireJobSecret crons, signature-verified webhooks, HMAC extension routes), so there is NO live gap — but adding one route to the 7600-line flipdesk-ebay.ts with a path outside the allowlist ships it UNAUTHENTICATED with no test failure. Use a /* wildcard with an explicit skip-list.
Add a rate limiter to /api/support/assistant/* (an LLM route with none) for consistency with every other AI surface.
userStories.notes: [P2][Security/Testing] Found 2026-07-18 by the security deep dive. CRITICAL CONTEXT so this is not misread as a breach: the audit traced all 740 .from() call sites on multi-tenant tables, taint-traced request-supplied ids into filters, and machine-diffed every mounted route against the middleware tables — and could NOT confirm a single cross-tenant data hole. Every unscoped-LOOKING query hand-verified as parent-verified (inventory_items!inner(user_id), loadListingOwned, loadReconcilePair, or a locally-minted id). The US-268 discipline is genuinely being followed. This story closes the TEST gap and inverts a default that currently makes unauthenticated exposure a silent one-line mistake. | 2026-07-18 THREE OF FOUR ACs (agent loop). AC4 DONE: /api/support/assistant/* now carries rateLimiter(20/min) — it was the only AI surface with none. Not an open faucet before (support-assistant.ts calls loadGateAndDecide before any token spend) but every other AI route is limited, and defence-in-depth belongs on the path where a loop costs money per iteration. AC1 PARTIAL, and the probe SHAPE had to change: /api/account/export and /delete take NO resource id — they act on the caller — so assertDenied is meaningless for them and there is nothing to point at tenant A. The property that a leak would actually trip is CONTAINMENT, so the new case asserts B's own export (200, must succeed) contains NONE of A's seeded ids across the seven tables it reads. Uses EXISTING required fixture ids, so it runs in CI immediately rather than waiting on a seed change. Also added an env-gated remove-bg probe (that route writes to the PUBLIC item-photos bucket, so a cross-tenant call would publish another seller's photo) — deliberately NOT added to REQUIRED_RESOURCE_IDS, because a case that hard-fails CI before the seed script provides TEST_USER_A_PHOTO_ID would simply get muted, which is worse than skipping loudly. Plus an unauthenticated-read probe on equity. ⚠ /api/account/delete is deliberately NOT probed and I want that recorded rather than looking like an oversight: the only cross-tenant shape is 'can B redirect the delete at A', and every way of asking risks destroying a fixture account if the answer is ever wrong — a test whose failure mode is data loss is not worth its signal. The route reads only c.get('userId') and accepts no target id; that is the property to preserve in review. AC2 DONE (documented: /api/admin/* is authorization-gated by adminAuthMiddleware at main.ts:730-731, so it is lower priority by design, not by neglect). AC3 — I DELIBERATELY DID NOT DO WHAT THE AC ASKED, and this is the judgement call to review. The AC says invert to app.use('/api/flipdesk/ebay/*', authMiddleware) + skip-list. I first VERIFIED the premise myself rather than trusting the audit: of 81 declared eBay routes, exactly 6 fall outside the 33 allowlist patterns, and I read every one — 5 are requireJobSecret crons, 1 is the OAuth callback verified by its single-use state token. So there is NO live gap, confirming the audit independently. The inversion is probably the right end state, but it re-wires auth for 81 live routes including OAuth returns and five Coolify crons, and it CANNOT be verified from here: a wrong skip-list 401s every cron and the eBay OAuth return in production, silently, until someone tries to reconnect an account. So I shipped the property the inversion exists FOR, at zero deployment risk: ebay-auth-coverage_test.ts fails the build if any eBay route is neither auth-covered nor listed in SELF_AUTHENTICATING with its mechanism NAMED. A second test re-verifies each exemption against the handler, so an exemption that stops being true (mechanism removed) also fails — a stale exemption is a documented promise the code no longer keeps. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by injecting an unauthenticated GET /secret-seller-report: the guard names it and fails; removing it passes. The middleware inversion remains worth doing BEHIND A STAGING DEPLOY — it is not worth doing blind, and it is now safe to defer because the silent-exposure path is closed. Verified: deno check + lint clean, 4169 edge tests pass. STILL passes:false: the new tenant cases only prove themselves when the tenant-isolation workflow runs with its two-tenant fixture (they skip locally by design), and AC3's inversion is deferred rather than done.

userStories.title: Android is a plumbing skeleton, but its README and 19 passing stories claim near-parity
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want the Android backlog to reflect reality. Android has genuinely good infrastructure — auth, a Room sync engine, mutation queue, delete reconciliation, telemetry, app-lock, CameraX capture, ~70 Kotlin files. It has no product: every navigation destination except one is a literal placeholder (ui/shell/AppShell.kt:162-175 — Home, Inventory, Money, Marketplaces, Settings, Details intake, AutoLister all render SectionPlaceholder; only capture/photos is real). Corroborating: Android calls exactly ONE edge endpoint in the entire codebase (/api/flipdesk/photo-profiles) versus iOS's 77 and web's ~530 — no grading submit, no inventory read, no eBay, no payments. Two documentation problems compound it: android/README.md:31-39 presents a package map for grading / inventory / marketplaces / money / billing whose directories contain ZERO .kt files, and :3 calls it 'at iOS parity'. And 19 stories are marked passes:true with no implementing code — verified: US-1380 Glance widgets (zero 'glance' references anywhere, no AppWidgetProvider in the manifest), US-1378 FCM push (no FirebaseMessaging reference), US-1383 Settings (routes to a placeholder), US-1384/1385/1387/1388/1389, US-1393 localization (no values-* locale dirs). The pattern is clean: US-1300-1328 (infrastructure) are genuinely done; US-1378-1396 is a contiguous block marked done without code.
acceptanceCriteria: Re-open the falsely-passing Android stories (start with the verified list: US-1380, US-1378, US-1383, US-1384, US-1385, US-1387, US-1388, US-1389, US-1393) and audit the rest of the US-1378-1396 block the same way.
Correct android/README.md — remove the 'at iOS parity' claim and the package map for directories that contain no code. This is the first document a new engineer or a diligence reviewer reads.
Re-baseline the Android estimate: real completion is closer to 29/98 than the 48/98 the backlog implies, and ALL remaining work is the expensive UI/feature half rather than a polish pass.
Decide explicitly whether Android is on the launch plan. If it is, the remaining work is essentially the whole app.
userStories.notes: [P1][Android/Backlog-integrity] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. This is the same class as US-1996 (archived stories marked passes:true that were explicitly DEFERRED) but larger and on a platform nobody is looking at. The state is more misleading than a plain stub would be: sophisticated offline-sync infrastructure attached to zero features reads as 'nearly done' to anyone who opens the project and sees the hard parts solved. NOT verified: whether the 50 OPEN Android stories are correctly open — only the passing ones were falsified. | [2026-07-27] AC1 DONE: audited the whole US-1378..1396 block, not just the verified subset — 14 stories re-opened as never-implemented (1378/1379/1380/1381/1382/1384/1385/1386/1387/1388/1389/1390/1392/1393) and 2 re-opened as partial (1391 has no signing config; 1395 has no androidTest/E2E). US-1383 was falsely passing and is now genuinely implemented. AC2 DONE: android/README.md no longer claims iOS parity, the package map lists only packages that contain code, and a Status section names what is and is not built. AC3 DONE: the table in that README is the re-baseline. AC4 (is Android on the launch plan?) is STILL OPEN — that is a product decision, not an engineering one.

userStories.title: iOS silently omits the entire paid consumer grading path, including the 14-day dispute flow
userStories.description: As a consumer grading on iOS, I want the same journey the web offers. There are TWO independent grading pipelines in the edge: the consumer/certified path (routes/grade.ts:209 /submit, :751 /pay/:id, :837 /status/:id, :1117 /dispute) and the FlipDesk/reseller path (/api/flipdesk/grading/{validate,submit,submissions/:id}). Web implements BOTH (new-submission.tsx:647, bulk-submission.tsx:332, submission-detail.tsx:244). iOS implements ONLY the FlipDesk path — Grading/GradingService.swift:6,55 documents and calls validate -> submit -> GET /submissions/:id — and grepping iOS for grade/pay, grade/status and grade/dispute returns NOTHING. So iOS has no consumer certified-grading submission, no per-grade payment flow, and NO GRADE DISPUTE FLOW at all.
acceptanceCriteria: Decide explicitly whether the consumer grading path belongs on iOS. Nothing in IOS_PARITY_AUDIT.md or the Android plan mentions this omission either way, which is weak evidence it is accidental rather than a product decision — settle it in writing.
If it belongs: implement submit / pay / status / dispute on iOS against routes/grade.ts.

If it does not: document why, and confirm the dispute obligation is discharged some other way — a 14-day dispute window that only one client can exercise is a support and chargeback liability regardless of intent.
Any parity matrix must stop treating 'grading submission' as ONE row; scoring it that way marks iOS complete while the entire paid consumer path is missing.
userStories.notes: [P1][iOS/Parity] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. Two implementations of the core revenue journey is the highest-value drift surface in the repo, and the mobile client omits the paid half. The dispute gap is the sharpest edge: US-1340 tracks a 14-day dispute window as a real obligation, and a user who graded on iOS has no in-app route to exercise it.

userStories.title: Legal ToS/privacy versions are hardcoded in both clients while the server derives them from the DB — and iOS has no re-acceptance gate
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want consent records to name the version the user actually saw. The edge derives current legal versions DYNAMICALLY from DB rows (lib/legal-versions.ts:66, consumed at routes/legal.ts:73,105,162). Both clients HARDCODE them: ios/GradeThread/Auth/AuthStore.swift:19-20 (legalTosVersion / legalPrivacyVersion = '2026-04-01') and src/lib/constants.ts:1491-1494 (LEGAL_VERSIONS). The only sync mechanism is a code comment (AuthStore.swift:17-18, 'Keep IN SYNC with the web ... and the edge mirror') with no automated guard. Worse, iOS has NO re-acceptance gate at all: web has src/components/auth/legal-gate.tsx; iOS never calls /api/legal (0 matches).
acceptanceCriteria: Clients must READ the current version from the server rather than hardcoding it, or a build-time guard must fail when the constants disagree with the DB-backed source.
Implement a re-acceptance gate on iOS equivalent to legal-gate.tsx.
Add a test/guard covering the three-way agreement (edge DB, web constants, iOS constants) — a comment is not a mechanism.
userStories.notes: [P1][Compliance/Legal] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. The failure mode is silent and legally material: the moment an operator publishes a new ToS row via admin-legal.ts, web and iOS signups keep recording 2026-04-01 — users are attested to a version they were never shown, and iOS users are never re-prompted at all. That is a defensible-consent failure, and exactly what an enterprise or legal review looks for. | 2026-07-18 SCOPED DOWN + GUARD ADDED (agent loop). ⚠ THIS STORY OVERSTATED THE RISK and the correction matters more than the fix. It claims users are 'attested to a version they were never shown'. For the WEB that is not what happens: legal-gate.tsx does NOT trust the hardcoded constant — it asks /api/legal/status (its own comment says so at :29) — and /api/legal/accept stamps the SERVER's current versions (legal.ts:103-106), never a client-supplied value. So after a FORCING republish the system SELF-CORRECTS: the gate fires and an immutable legal_acceptances row is written with the real version. The genuine residual hole is narrower and does NOT self-correct: on a MINOR republish (requires_reacceptance:false) requiredSince deliberately does not advance, so the gate correctly stays quiet — while handle_new_user (00142:79) still records the CLIENT-SUPPLIED constant into users.tos_accepted_version. The new user was shown the live document (/terms serves current) but their record names an older version, and nothing later corrects it. Moderate, not the defensible-consent failure described. FIXED WHAT IS FIXABLE HERE: added src/lib/__tests__/legal-versions-lockstep.test.ts pinning the baseline across all THREE projects that hold it — web LEGAL_VERSIONS, edge FALLBACK_TOS/PRIVACY_VERSION, and iOS AuthStore.legalTosVersion/legalPrivacyVersion — plus a shape check so a placeholder value cannot silently disable the gate. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED from every direction: drifting the web constant fails 2 assertions, drifting the iOS constant fails 1. That iOS assertion is the valuable one — Swift cannot be compiled on a Windows checkout, so a source-level check is the ONLY cross-project verification available for it. STILL passing:false on the two real ACs: (1) the durable fix is for the server to stamp the version at signup rather than trusting client metadata — that is a migration to handle_new_user and I did not want to stack a third held one; (2) iOS still has NO re-acceptance gate at all (grep for api/legal across ios/ returns nothing), which remains the largest genuine gap in this story and needs a macOS session. [2026-07-19 AC3 DONE + AC1 GUARD HALF. AC2 NEEDS macOS — story stays open] AC3 was the whole point of the story (a comment is not a mechanism) and is now real: src/test/legal-version-parity.test.ts asserts the THREE-WAY agreement between the edge fallbacks (FALLBACK_TOS_VERSION / FALLBACK_PRIVACY_VERSION), web LEGAL_VERSIONS, and the iOS AuthStore.swift static lets, by parsing each source. Negative-verified by bumping the iOS constant to 2026-09-01 — the guard fails naming all three values. AC1: took the guard option the AC explicitly allows rather than making clients read /api/legal at runtime. A build-time comparison against the live DB is not possible (no DB at build), and the edge FALLBACK constants are the DB-backed sources checked-in form, so this pins what CAN be pinned. Making the clients dynamic remains the stronger fix and is still open. Also asserted the versions are ISO dates: the edge ORDERS versions to decide whether re-acceptance is required, so a free-form string would break that comparison silently. And the parse-succeeded guard is explicit, because comparing null to null would have passed vacuously — it caught a real bug immediately when a heredoc ate the backslashes in my regex and both parsers returned null. AC2 NOT DONE and deliberately not faked: iOS has no re-acceptance gate (never calls /api/legal) while web has legal-gate.tsx. I cannot build or test Swift on Windows, and writing a compliance gate blind is precisely the wrong place for that. A test asserts the gap STILL EXISTS so it flips the moment someone implements it, rather than the story looking complete because the parity guard is green. AuthStore.swift now documents the gap in place. Seventh prose-matching guard failure this session: my new Swift comment names /api/legal, which the absence assertion matched. Comments are stripped now. | 2026-07-19 ⚠ STALE HELD-MIGRATION CLAIM — do not act on it. The migration(s) this note calls HELD (00142) are all on origin/main, verified individually with git log origin/main against each file rather than inferred from the linter's summary. The standing rule makes this decisive: a commit containing a migration is NOT pushed until the operator has applied the SQL, so a migration present on origin/main was pushed, which means its hold was already released. PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md agrees — every entry through 00490 (the highest migration in the tree) is marked APPLIED and confirmed by the user, so nothing is genuinely pending. WHY THIS MATTERS ENOUGH TO CORRECT: a stale hold tells the next reader the branch is frozen when it is not, which either invites a pointless prod session or — worse — makes them hold back an unrelated push that was always safe. Correction APPENDED rather than edited into the original sentence, because these notes are append-only and the history of what was believed when is itself worth keeping.

userStories.title: Three fully-built marketplace OAuth connectors (Depop/Etsy/Whatnot) are live with zero callers
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we do not want live token-minting endpoints with no product behind them. 937 lines of production OAuth code have no caller on any client: routes/flipdesk-depop.ts (388 lines, /oauth/start:80, /oauth/callback:127, /oauth/refresh:216, /disconnect:226), flipdesk-etsy.ts (311 lines), flipdesk-whatnot.ts (238 lines) — web 0, iOS 0, extension 0. All three are mounted and live (main.ts:1049-1051). They are also HALF connectors: OAuth plus disconnect only, no publish/revise, so even with UI they could not list. Also uncalled by any client: /api/drip, /api/campaign-track, /api/changelog.
acceptanceCriteria: Decide per connector: gate behind a feature flag, or delete. Live authenticated endpoints that mint and store marketplace tokens are attack surface and an audit finding with zero offsetting value while unreachable.
If keeping them for a near-term launch, say so in the story and add the missing publish/revise half — an OAuth-only connector cannot deliver the feature it implies.
Re-check /api/drip, /api/campaign-track and /api/changelog the same way (note /api/drip is separately in scope for the tenant-isolation test gap).
userStories.notes: [P2][Security/Dead-code] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. Related: US-1662 tracks Whatnot listing publish/update/delist as open, so the Whatnot OAuth half was likely built ahead of it — that is the benign reading. The security point stands regardless: unreachable-but-live token endpoints expand the attack surface without expanding the product, and they will be found in any diligence review. | 2026-07-19 RESOLVED — AND THE STORY'S SECURITY PREMISE WAS WRONG. I started implementing a mount-time gate, then checked whether one already existed before shipping it. It does. All three connectors are ALREADY gated off by default and fail CLOSED: isDepopEnabled() / isEtsyEnabled() / isWhatnotEnabled() each require an explicit *_ENABLED flag AND the OAuth credentials to be present, and every user-reachable handler checks the guard as its FIRST statement (verified by count: depop 7 handlers / 7 guards, etsy 6/6, whatnot 4/4). The only handler without a first-line guard is /oauth/refresh in each, which is requireJobSecret-gated (internal cron) and refreshes EXISTING connections — with the connector off there are none, so it is a no-op. So 'live token-minting endpoints' overstated it: the routes are mounted but cannot mint anything without a deliberate two-part operator action. Mounted-but-guarded is not the same as live, and the audit that produced this story did not distinguish them. I THREW AWAY MY OWN WORK RATHER THAN SHIP IT: a second env allowlist plus connector-gate.ts and 6 tests were written and then deleted, because a third gating mechanism over two existing ones is precisely the duplication this backlog keeps paying for — and a redundant gate is worse than none, since the next reader has to check all three to know whether a connector is on. AC1 is therefore already satisfied by DEPOP_ENABLED/ETSY_ENABLED/WHATNOT_ENABLED; no code change. AC2 stands as real remaining work and is correctly tracked elsewhere — these are still OAuth-only half-connectors, and US-1662 owns the Whatnot publish/update/delist half. AC3 RE-CHECKED, and the 'uncalled by any client' framing does not survive contact either: /api/drip/tick is a REGISTERED CRON (cron-runs.ts, COOLIFY.md, job-secret authed), /api/campaign-track is hit by EMAIL CLIENTS by design (open pixel + click wrapper, deliberately unauthenticated), and only the PUBLIC /api/changelog feed is genuinely uncalled — the web app uses /api/admin/changelog instead — but it is an anonymous read-only feed of already-public entries, which is negligible surface and not worth gating. Grepping the repo for fetch() call sites is the wrong reachability test for cron endpoints and email-client endpoints; that is the methodology lesson worth keeping from this story.

userStories.title: 50+ documented lockstep mirrors are enforced by comments; only ONE has an automated guard
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want cross-platform contract drift to be caught by CI rather than by an incident. The repo is admirably self-aware — 50+ explicit mirror/lockstep markers exist (src/lib/constants.ts:1059-1061 'MUST stay in lockstep', autolister-verify-windows.ts:12-13, best-offer-thresholds.ts:1-6, grading-readiness.ts:6 'Client-side mirror of buildValidation()', cert-number.ts:16, grade-standard.ts:2,16, listing-origin.ts:3, garment-mapping.ts:6, constants.ts:565,1118,1440,1489). iOS adds a THIRD copy of many (AIExtract/AIExtractTypes.swift:3, AIItemFieldWriter.swift:14, Analytics/ListingPerformanceModels.swift:3,96,142, SourceROIRollup.swift:8,99). Exactly ONE has an automated guard — Class A storage, per IOS_PARITY_AUDIT.md:32-34 (item-photo-storage_test.ts). The edge test dir has just 4 guard tests (ads-guardrails, rls-guard, support-output-guard, us1507-relist-guard), none covering the pricing, grading-readiness or legal-version mirrors.
acceptanceCriteria: Generalize the Class A pattern: for each high-risk mirror, add a shared behavioural FIXTURE asserted by every copy's suite (the remedy US-1995 already applied to title-sync), rather than source-diffing.
Prioritize the mirrors where divergence is silent and expensive: grading-readiness (buildValidation), best-offer thresholds, pricing constants, legal versions (see the legal story), grade-standard.
IOS_PARITY_AUDIT.md:80-84 already names this fix ('Source-guards for contracts — cheap, deterministic') and it was never generalized beyond Class A. Close that out.
userStories.notes: [P2][Architecture/Testing] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. The repo's OWN post-mortem (IOS_PARITY_AUDIT.md:11-20) says all three bugs in the original cluster were exactly this class, missed because unit tests pass on both sides independently while the seam diverges. This session hit the same pattern twice more: US-1995 (edge title-sync mirror with zero callers) and the ai-size-estimate-core dead copy. A comment asserting a link is not the link. | 2026-07-18 SECOND MIRROR PINNED — grading-readiness (agent loop). Following the same shape as the weighted-grade fixture (US-2041) earlier today. The edge's readiness rules were inline inside buildValidation, so the web mirror (previewGradingReadiness) could not be compared to anything; the two were held together by a comment stating 'the blocker STRINGS below are verbatim copies of the server's'. Extracted gradingReadinessBlockers() as a PURE exported function in flipdesk-grading.ts, had buildValidation call it (no behaviour change), and added src/test/fixtures/grading-readiness-cases.json — 13 cases asserted by BOTH suites. WHY THIS MIRROR RANKED HIGH: divergence is silent in BOTH directions and both are expensive — a client saying READY when the server disagrees sends a seller into a submit-time rejection, and a client saying NOT READY when the server would accept blocks them from paying us. The fixture deliberately covers the semantic edge that the copy exists to make: a 'defect' photo does NOT satisfy the fabric close-up requirement, because the pipeline ABSTAINS without a real weave/knit shot — if that rule drifts, a seller pays for a grade that comes back ungraded. Also pinned the exact blocker STRINGS, since the web card regex-matches them (onlyGarmentBlocks), making them a cross-project contract rather than mere copy. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED FROM BOTH SIDES independently: renaming 'Missing garment_type' to 'Missing garment type' in the WEB copy fails the vitest guard; deleting the fabric-close-up rule from the EDGE authority fails the deno guard. Restoring passes both. Verified: tsc clean, eslint 0 errors, 2242 vitest + 4188 deno tests pass. STILL passes:false — AC2 names five priority mirrors and two are now pinned (grade-standard/weights via US-2041, grading-readiness here). Remaining: best-offer thresholds, pricing constants, and legal versions (the last is US-2017 and is the compliance-sensitive one — clients hardcode a version the server derives from the DB). | 2026-07-18 AC2 COMPLETE — all five priority mirrors pinned (agent loop). Best-offer thresholds is the last: src/test/fixtures/best-offer-threshold-cases.json (14 cases) asserted by BOTH src/lib/__tests__/best-offer-thresholds.test.ts and services/edge-functions/src/tests/best-offer-parity_test.ts. The fixture targets the CONSTRAINT BOUNDARIES rather than happy paths, because that is where a drift changes behaviour: accept exactly AT list (nudged to one cent under), accept above list, a 1-cent listing that leaves no room for any accept, decline equal to accept, decline above accept, decline at/above list with no accept, zero and negative overrides, and fractional cents. These constraints are EBAY'S, not ours — eBay REJECTS a publish where autoAcceptPrice is not strictly below the listing price — so a drift means the composer cheerfully SAVES thresholds that fail at publish, after the seller believes they are finished. Also pinned the deliberate product behaviour that an inverted decline is DROPPED rather than silently rewritten: quietly 'fixing' a seller's number to satisfy eBay would change a figure they chose without telling them. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED from both sides: removing the accept-below-list clamp from the WEB mirror fails 2 vitest assertions; removing the inverted-decline drop from the EDGE authority fails the deno guard. ⚠ TWO THINGS WORTH RECORDING. (1) The two copies' TYPES differed subtly — the edge declares all five inputs required-but-nullable — so my first fixture (omitting keys) only type-checked against the web mirror. Supplying all five explicitly removed a cast AND made the table usable by both. (2) `tsc -b` caught an incomplete input in my own new test that VITEST had passed, because vitest does not typecheck. A test suite going green is not the same as the test being well-formed. FIVE OF FIVE now pinned: grade weights + rounding (US-2041), grading-readiness, legal versions (US-2017), pricing/credit-packs (US-2075), best-offer thresholds. AC1's broader sweep of the remaining ~45 documented mirrors is still open, but the five the audit named as highest-risk are done. | 2026-07-18 AC1 + AC3 DONE — story complete (agent loop). Rather than hand-fixing the remaining ~45 mirrors (≈45 commits, and the NEXT one would still be unguarded), added src/lib/__tests__/lockstep-registry.test.ts: it DISCOVERS every file whose comments assert a lockstep relationship and forces each to be classified as PINNED (a named fixture/test asserts both copies) or EXEMPT (with a stated reason ≥60 chars, enforced). Same shape as SERVICE_ROLE_ONLY in rls-guard_test.ts — a NEW mirror fails the build by name until a human decides which it is. That converts an unbounded manual backlog into a bounded, self-maintaining one. Three sub-guards: unclassified-file detection, a STALE-ENTRY check (a registry naming files that no longer declare a mirror rots into noise and hides which entries are load-bearing), and an EXEMPT-must-justify check. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by adding a throwaway file containing 'client mirror of … keep the two in lockstep': the guard failed and named it; removing it passed. ⚠ THE CLASSIFICATION WAS DONE BY READING EACH FILE, not by pattern-matching, and the distinctions are the actual content. EXEMPT is not 'unimportant' — each entry names why a drift is RECOVERABLE: use-buyer-entitlements mirrors subscription statuses the server re-checks on every gated action; verified.ts mirrors a rule ALSO enforced by a DB CHECK (00057), so a drift yields a rejected write rather than bad data; signup.tsx's password mirror is explicitly non-authoritative and the policy itself is pinned elsewhere; autolister.tsx is an intra-file CSS value, not cross-project at all; publish-preflight mirrors something WITHIN the edge project where an ordinary import test suffices. And ebay-prefill.ts turned out to be the best-guarded of the lot — its registry is GENERATED from the edge via `npm run sync:aspects` with a CI drift guard, i.e. the data cannot be hand-edited out of sync at all, which is a stronger mechanism than any fixture. Also had to exclude the guard file from its own scan (it documents the marker phrases in order to search for them). NOW passes:true: AC1 (generalized), AC2 (all five priority mirrors pinned), AC3 (IOS_PARITY_AUDIT's 'source-guards for contracts' closed out). | 2026-07-19 ⚠ STALE HELD-MIGRATION CLAIM — do not act on it. The migration(s) this note calls HELD (00057) are all on origin/main, verified individually with git log origin/main against each file rather than inferred from the linter's summary. The standing rule makes this decisive: a commit containing a migration is NOT pushed until the operator has applied the SQL, so a migration present on origin/main was pushed, which means its hold was already released. PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md agrees — every entry through 00490 (the highest migration in the tree) is marked APPLIED and confirmed by the user, so nothing is genuinely pending. WHY THIS MATTERS ENOUGH TO CORRECT: a stale hold tells the next reader the branch is frozen when it is not, which either invites a pointless prod session or — worse — makes them hold back an unrelated push that was always safe. Correction APPENDED rather than edited into the original sentence, because these notes are append-only and the history of what was believed when is itself worth keeping.

userStories.title: Three browser extensions are maintained in parallel against the same marketplace DOMs
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want one extension to maintain, not three. Three separate MV3 extensions are all receiving active commits: extension (Lister, v0.1.0, last commit 2026-07-13), extension-condition (Condition Check, v0.2.1, 2026-07-15) and extension-unified ('Grade & List', v0.3.5, 2026-07-18). The name 'unified' implies it supersedes the other two, but both predecessors are still getting feature work — extension-condition received US-1884 accessibility work on 07-15.
acceptanceCriteria: Confirm whether extension and extension-condition are deprecated in favour of extension-unified. If so, freeze them and stop investing.

If all three ship, document why — three Chrome Web Store listings mean three review cycles and three selector-maintenance burdens against the same marketplace DOMs, which is the expensive part when a marketplace changes its markup.
Cross-check against US-1872 (unified extension epic) and US-1881 (Firefox/Edge support), which assume a single artifact.
userStories.notes: [P3][Extension/Maintenance] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. Likely a migration in progress rather than a mistake — filed so the migration gets finished deliberately instead of leaving three live artifacts drifting apart. | 2026-07-19 DONE — all three ACs answered, and the investigation turned up a LIVE USER-FACING BUG that the story only predicted as a risk. AC1 CONFIRMED, and the confirmation already existed: extension-unified/README.md records a founder decision of 2026-07-09 deprecating both predecessors, and US-1872 AC5 already owns deleting them. So the question was settled six days before this story was filed — what was missing is that NOTHING MARKED the legacy folders, so they kept attracting work. Both READMEs now carry a deprecation banner stating the rule (bug fixes only, and apply every fix to the unified copy in the SAME commit). AC2 answered where the decision actually lives — scripts/package-extensions.mjs still builds three store zips, so the why-three reasoning is now a comment there, including the condition that ends it. AC3 cross-checked: US-1872 AC5 is gated on parity and parity is NOT reached (US-1880/1881/1882/1883 open), so deleting the folders now would be wrong; US-1881 Firefox assumes the single artifact and is consistent with that sequencing. THE FINDING: I checked whether the hand-sync was actually holding, rather than assuming. extension-condition is byte-identical to its unified counterpart — that half held. The Lister had DRIFTED, and not cosmetically: US-1875 AC1 fixed a Poshmark delist probe that required both `menu` and `remove` BEFORE any interaction, when `remove` does not exist until `menu` is clicked, which runDelistFlow does AFTER the probe. Traced it through extension/content/common.js to be sure rather than reasoning from the version bump: the probe is unsatisfiable, so the shipped legacy Lister's auto-delist failed on EVERY run. Worst part is the error text — "Poshmark's page changed ... the GradeThread Lister needs an update" — so a bug of ours read as a marketplace change, which is presumably why nobody chased it for four days. Ported the fix to all three legacy delist blocks. WHY FIX A DEPRECATED FOLDER: it is still packaged and still installed by real users, and "stop investing" means stop adding features, not ship a known-broken flow until the store listing is retired. NEW GUARD extension-unified/test/legacy-parity.test.cjs, scoped deliberately narrow — it compares the delist PROBE CONTRACT, not the files, because the two trees legitimately differ (the unified copy carries `verify` blocks the legacy runtime does not implement) and a whole-file diff would be permanently red and would get switched off, which is how guards die. It asserts BOTH the parity AND the invariant independently, so a wrong change applied consistently to both copies still fails. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED both directions: reintroducing the bug in the legacy copy alone trips the drift assertion, reintroducing it in BOTH trips the invariant assertion. One implementation note worth keeping: the two selector trees are evaluated in separate vm realms, so deepStrictEqual fails on identical content ("actual: ['menu'], expected: ['menu']") because Array prototypes differ across realms — compared as JSON instead. Verified: 14/14 extension tests, 2462 web tests, packaging still produces all three zips.

userStories.title: email_deliveries stores full rendered email bodies forever with no purge
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want the email log bounded. 00095_email_deliveries.sql:9-24 stores recipient, subject and 'html text not null' — the complete rendered body — for every critical send, with rows kept at status sent/dead_letter. There is NO purge anywhere: the only pruning in lib/data-retention.ts:132 is cron_runs (30-day window). No DELETE FROM email_deliveries exists in the codebase.
acceptanceCriteria: Extend the data-retention cron: delete sent rows older than ~90 days, and null out html on dead_letter rows once triaged.
Coordinate with the GDPR erasure story — this table is the single largest reservoir of un-erasable PII (it is email-keyed, so the deletion cascade never reaches it).

Note the operational cost too: one full HTML document per critical email, forever, becomes the largest table in the DB and inflates backup and restore windows — which directly worsens the RTO in the backup story.
userStories.notes: [P3][DB/Growth] Found 2026-07-18 by the data-integrity deep dive. Compounds three other findings at once: GDPR erasure (un-erasable PII), backup/restore duration (RTO), and the stalled retention sweep (the cron that would own this purge is itself not advancing). The partial index email_deliveries_due_idx (:31-33) stays healthy while the heap does not, so query performance will not warn you. | 2026-07-18 FIXED (agent loop). AC1 DONE, with TWO DIFFERENT RULES rather than the one the AC implied — the distinction matters and is the whole risk of this change: (1) status='sent' rows are pure history once delivered, so they are DELETED after 90 days (well past any support window that would need to re-read what a user was actually sent); (2) status='dead_letter' rows are an OPERATOR REPLAY QUEUE and are NEVER deleted — only their heavy PII-bearing `html` body is stripped, and on a longer 180-day window so a genuine replay stays possible. Deleting dead-letters would destroy the evidence that mail went UNDELIVERED, which is the entire purpose of a dead-letter table; the careless version of this fix (one unscoped DELETE) would have quietly eaten that queue while looking like a successful cleanup. Both cutoffs are named constants with the reasoning inline. Wired into the existing data-retention cron next to the cron_runs prune, and best-effort for the same stated reason — a prune hiccup must never fail the PII purge that is the job's reason to exist. THREE NEW TESTS in data-retention_test.ts, all NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by simulating the exact careless edits: removing .eq('status','sent') fails the scoping test, and switching the dead-letter .update({html:''}) to .delete() fails the body-strip test; restoring passes. Checked against the repo gotcha too — no .or() on an UPDATE/DELETE (US-1552), only .eq/.lt/.neq, so this cannot hit the self-hosted PostgREST 42703 that CI would not catch. Verified: deno check + lint clean, 4167 edge tests pass. AC2 CONTEXT: this directly reduces the un-erasable-PII reservoir called out in US-2005 (email_deliveries was its single largest contributor) and shrinks the backup/restore window that worsens the RTO in US-2002 — the three findings were compounding each other. STILL passes:false on AC3's quantification: how much this actually reclaims, and how much accumulated while there was no purge at all, needs a prod query (select pg_total_relation_size('public.email_deliveries'), count(*) filter (where status='sent' and created_at < now() - interval '90 days')). Worth running BEFORE the first sweep so the reclaim is measured rather than assumed, and worth knowing that the first run will be a large delete on a table nobody has ever pruned. | 2026-07-19 FOLLOW-UP: THE SWEEP IS NOW BOUNDED. AC1 shipped previously and AC2 is satisfied (email_deliveries IS covered by the account-delete email-keyed purge at account.ts:564, so the un-erasable reservoir is addressed from both ends). What the previous pass flagged in its own closing line but did not fix: 'the first run will be a large delete on a table nobody has ever pruned'. That was left as an unbounded DELETE over the entire historical backlog — a long transaction and a WAL spike on what is on track to be the largest table in the DB, running in a nightly cron on a SINGLE-REPLICA edge with no graceful shutdown until today. Both sweeps now select at most EMAIL_PURGE_BATCH (5,000) ids and mutate by id. A capped run is not a lost run: the cron is daily, so a backlog drains over consecutive nights and each night's work stays predictable. IMPLEMENTED AS scan-then-mutate-by-id RATHER THAN A LIMIT ON THE MUTATION, deliberately: per the US-1552 gotcha, the self-hosted prod PostgREST and the newer local stack disagree about what they accept on UPDATE/DELETE, so CI structurally cannot catch a regression there — two plain statements are version-proof. The run now also REPORTS what it did (email_sent_purged / email_bodies_stripped / email_purge_batch), because a capped run that reports nothing is indistinguishable from a no-op, and those counts are how an operator knows whether the backlog is still draining. REWROTE TWO EXISTING TESTS RATHER THAN LOOSENING THEM: they asserted the old source shape (.update chained directly to .eq) which the batching necessarily changed. The INTENT was right and is preserved — scoping is now asserted on the SCAN, which is the same property since the mutation only ever receives ids that query produced — plus a new test that both sweeps carry the cap. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED all three by simulating the exact careless edits: removing the limits, unscoping the sent purge, and switching the dead-letter strip to a delete each turn the suite red; restoring returns it to zero. STILL passes:false on AC3 alone: how much this reclaims needs a prod query (select pg_total_relation_size('public.email_deliveries'), count(*) filter (where status='sent' and created_at < now() - interval '90 days')), and it is worth running BEFORE the first sweep so the reclaim is measured rather than assumed. Verified: edge 4273 passed, deno check + lint clean.

userStories.title: Consignor payouts are never reversed when the sale is later returned or refunded
userStories.description: As a seller, when a consigned item comes back I must not be out the consignor's cut. lib/consignor-payout.ts:105 gates NEW payouts on sale.status === 'completed', but there is NO reversal path for one already settled. flipdesk-ebay.ts:3626 flips sales.status to returned/refunded on an eBay return or approved cancellation and restores the inventory item — and touches nothing in consignor_payouts. Once fireTransfer (consignor-payout.ts:322-335) has moved money to the consignor's Connect account and set status='paid', SETTLED_STATUSES (consignor-payout-math.ts:69) makes every later evaluation return skip('already_settled'). A repo-wide grep for 'clawback' finds it in the affiliate, Stripe-metadata, Apple and Google paths — nothing in the consignor engine.
acceptanceCriteria: On the sale-status transition to returned/refunded (flipdesk-ebay.ts:3626 and any other writer), look up consignor_payouts for the affected sale_id(s).

Cancel pending/failed rows outright; for PAID rows either issue a Stripe transfers.createReversal (idempotency-keyed on the payout id, matching the existing consignor_payout_ key convention) or write a negative-balance row that offsets the consignor's next payout. Pick one and say why in the notes.
Consider a hold window before transfer, mirroring the affiliate engine's hold_days — the cheapest fix for most of this exposure is not paying out until the return window closes.
Surface it: a paid payout on a returned sale must appear somewhere an operator sees, because today the row stays 'paid' and nothing signals the loss.
userStories.notes: [P1][Money/Consignment] Found 2026-07-18 by the money-correctness deep dive. LARGEST PER-INCIDENT DOLLAR EXPOSURE in the codebase: a $200 consigned item at a 60% split transfers $120 to the consignor; the buyer returns it 20 days later and eBay refunds them $200 from the seller. The seller eats $120 with no automated recovery and NO SIGNAL — the payout row still reads 'paid'. Note the shape: this is not a bug in the payout engine, which is well built (pre-flight transfer lookup defeats Stripe's 24h key TTL, math is separated and tested). It is a MISSING EDGE between two subsystems that each work correctly on their own. Source-only finding: the Stripe MCP connector needs authorization, so live transfer/reversal state was not checked. | 2026-07-19 FIXED. THE DECISION AC2 ASKED FOR: Stripe transfers.createReversal, not a negative-balance offset — and the deciding argument was not preference. consignor_payouts.amount carries CHECK (amount >= 0) from migration 00171, so a negative row cannot be written without dropping a constraint that is otherwise protecting the ledger; and an offset only recovers money if the consignor HAS a next payout, which for the one-off consignor of a returned item means it recovers nothing and quietly becomes bad debt with no owner. Reversal returns funds immediately and reads as the exact inverse of the original transfer. Idempotency key consignor_reversal_<payoutId>, matching the existing consignor_payout_<id> convention. THE FAILURE MODE IS HANDLED, NOT IGNORED: a reversal fails when the connected account already withdrew the funds. That is what the new clawback_pending status is for — the row stops claiming 'paid', records reversal_error, logs at error, and raises a CRITICAL ops event. Leaving it on 'paid' is precisely the silent loss this story existed to end, so 'paid' now means only 'paid for a sale that stood'. WIRED INTO EVERY WRITER, not just the one the story cited: ebay applyOutcomeToSale (the Post-Order return/cancel path at :3626), ebay ORDER SYNC (an order re-synced as CANCELED/FULLY_REFUNDED — this one was not in the AC and is arguably the likelier real-world trigger, since most refunds are discovered by the sweep rather than through the Post-Order UI), plus depop-orders, etsy-orders and shopify-orders, which all share an identical refund-status shape. reverseConsignorPayoutsForSales is idempotent (reversed/canceled rows skip), so overlapping paths cannot double-reverse — that mattered because the eBay Post-Order path and the order sweep genuinely do overlap. AC3 HOLD WINDOW IMPLEMENTED BUT SHIPS OFF (hold_days: 0 = today's behaviour). It is the cheapest mitigation — no transfer means nothing to claw back — but turning it on delays when real people get paid and may contradict terms a seller already agreed with their consignors, so it is the seller's policy call and not a default I should make for them. The hold is measured from the SALE date, not from row creation, so a sale the sweep picks up late does not get a window starting weeks after the buyer received the item. AC4 SURFACED three ways: the CRITICAL ops event, the status itself, and a destructive badge in consignment.tsx. TYPESCRIPT CAUGHT A REAL DRIFT MID-CHANGE: there were TWO status lists — CONSIGNOR_PAYOUT_STATUSES in constants.ts and ConsignorPayoutStatus in types/database.ts — and updating only the first produced a TS2367 'no overlap' error on the badge comparison rather than a silently dead branch. New pure module consignor-reversal-math.ts (planReversal + hold helpers) with 13 unit tests covering the headline $120-on-a-$200-return case, both spellings of cancelled, and the two cases that must never be silently dropped: paid-without-transfer-id, and an unknown status (cancelled rather than ignored — the worst case is a payout needing re-issue, versus money leaving for a dead sale). Verified: edge 4221 passed, web 2271 passed, tsc clean, lint 0 errors. MIGRATION 00481 IS HELD — and its enum-before-use ordering is called out in PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md, because the edge writes the new values at boot and applying late would break the money-recovery path specifically. | 2026-07-19 ⚠ STALE HELD-MIGRATION CLAIM — do not act on it. The migration(s) this note calls HELD (00171, 00481) are all on origin/main, verified individually with git log origin/main against each file rather than inferred from the linter's summary. The standing rule makes this decisive: a commit containing a migration is NOT pushed until the operator has applied the SQL, so a migration present on origin/main was pushed, which means its hold was already released. PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md agrees — every entry through 00490 (the highest migration in the tree) is marked APPLIED and confirmed by the user, so nothing is genuinely pending. WHY THIS MATTERS ENOUGH TO CORRECT: a stale hold tells the next reader the branch is frozen when it is not, which either invites a pointless prod session or — worse — makes them hold back an unrelated push that was always safe. Correction APPENDED rather than edited into the original sentence, because these notes are append-only and the history of what was believed when is itself worth keeping.

userStories.title: inventory.tsx paginates the grid, then loads the tenant's ENTIRE listings + sales history anyway
userStories.description: As a seller with real volume, opening Inventory must not download my whole commercial history. src/pages/inventory.tsx:156-159 issues supabase.from('listings').select('*') and supabase.from('sales').select('*') with NO limit, range or filter — only RLS tenant scoping. The grid itself IS correctly paginated (:229 uses .range(page*PAGE_SIZE)) and counts via count:'exact' (:203). The two unbounded reads exist only to build listingsByItem / saleByItem maps (:171-182) for a days-listed column on the ~50 visible rows. Same file :135-137 fetches inventory_items.select('brand') for EVERY row in the tenant just to populate a distinct-brand filter dropdown.
acceptanceCriteria: Scope both hydration queries to the page's item ids: .in('inventory_item_id', itemRows.map(r => r.id)), selecting only the columns the column needs (inventory_item_id, listed_at / sold_at). Both supporting indexes already exist (idx_listings_inventory_item_id, idx_sales_inventory_item_id).
Replace the whole-tenant brand scan with a distinct RPC or a maintained brand list.
Verify with a seeded heavy account (thousands of rows) that the Inventory payload is bounded by page size, not by account age.
userStories.notes: [P1][Perf/Frontend] Found 2026-07-18 by the query-performance deep dive (the pass the ops audit flagged as owed and explicitly NOT done). Concrete scenario: a seller with 5,000 listings and 3,000 sales pulls 8,000 WIDE rows (select('*') on two wide tables; sales carries fee/payout/tracking/buyer columns) into a browser to decorate 50 grid rows. Multi-MB payload plus main-thread JSON parse on the entry path to the app, and it grows monotonically forever because sales is append-only. staleTime 5min limits refetch frequency, not the first paint of every session. Highest value-to-effort ratio in the whole performance audit — roughly an hour's work. | 2026-07-18 FIXED (main finding) (agent loop). inventory.tsx no longer loads the tenant's entire listings + sales history. The hydration query moved AFTER the paginated page query and is now scoped .in('inventory_item_id', pageItemIds) and projected to the only TWO columns calcDaysListed actually reads (listed_at, sale_date) — down from select('*') on two wide tables with no bound at all. Payload is now proportional to PAGE_SIZE instead of to account age; both supporting indexes already existed. Narrowed the helper's parameter types to DaysListedListing/DaysListedSale so widening the projection later requires widening a type — a visible decision rather than silent drift. ⚠ CAUGHT WHILE FIXING: `items` was `data?.items ?? []`, a fresh array identity every render, and my new pageItemIds memo derives from it and feeds a queryKey. TanStack hashes keys structurally so this was NOT causing refetch churn — but eslint flagged it and relying on that hashing is incidental rather than obvious, so `items` is memoized. STILL passes:false on AC2: the distinct-brand dropdown at :132-137 STILL scans every inventory_items row in the tenant to produce ~200 strings. I left it deliberately — PostgREST cannot do DISTINCT without an RPC, and the available client-side workarounds (a limit, or sampling) would silently DROP brands from the filter, which is a correctness regression traded for a perf win. It needs the RPC, which means a migration, and I did not want to stack a third held migration. | 2026-07-19 AC2 DONE — the story is now complete. The distinct-brand dropdown no longer scans every inventory_items row in the tenant: migration 00482 adds inventory_distinct_brands(), and inventory.tsx calls it via supabase.rpc(). The previous pass left this deliberately, for two stated reasons, and both are now resolved: (1) 'it needs an RPC, which means a migration' — correct, and that is exactly what shipped, because the client-side alternatives (a LIMIT, or sampling) would silently DROP brands from the filter, which is a correctness regression traded for a perf win and therefore not an acceptable shortcut; (2) 'I did not want to stack a third held migration' — that constraint has lapsed, since 00480/00481/00482 now travel together and apply in one ordered pass. SECURITY NOTE worth keeping: the function is SECURITY INVOKER and takes NO user_id parameter. That is not an oversight — running as the caller means the existing RLS policy on inventory_items applies unchanged, so it cannot return another tenant's brands even if called directly with a forged argument. userStories.title: Bulk grading submit is an unbounded N+1 that can charge credits and then time out
userStories.description: As a seller bulk-grading, a large batch must not half-charge me. services/edge-functions/src/routes/flipdesk-grading.ts:419 loops `for (const item of validation.result.items)` and inside it (:490-494) issues a per-item item_photos SELECT — a strict regression against the validation pass in the SAME FILE, which at :193-197 already loads photo coverage for all items in ONE .in('inventory_item_id', itemIds) query with the comment 'Photo coverage — one query covering all items'. Each iteration also INSERTs a submission (:455-465), runs runPaymentPrecedence (:476, itself several queries), copies photos in storage, and inserts links — all sequential, no Promise.all. NOTHING BOUNDS THE BATCH: inputs.length is validated only for === 0 (:109) and submitBodySchema enforces no max that reaches this loop.
acceptanceCriteria: Cap the batch size at the schema, with a clear error when exceeded.
Hoist the item_photos fetch out of the loop, reusing the .in() pattern already present at :193.
Chunk the remaining per-item work with bounded concurrency rather than a fully sequential loop.

Address the partial-charge window: the loop sets charged = true at :487 BEFORE the photo copy, and the catch-block compensation handles a THROWN error, not a killed isolate. Decide what a timed-out batch owes the seller and make it recoverable.
userStories.notes: [P1][Perf/Money] Found 2026-07-18 by the query-performance deep dive. This one has a correctness dimension, not just latency: 200 selected items is ~1,000+ sequential round trips plus storage copies in a single request — near-certain edge timeout — and because credits are charged per item inside the loop, a timeout leaves a PARTIALLY CHARGED batch that the compensation path does not cover (it catches thrown errors; an isolate kill throws nothing). Fixing the N+1 also shrinks the window in which that can happen, but the charge/commit ordering deserves its own thought. | 2026-07-18 N+1 FIXED, AC1 WAS ALREADY TRUE (agent loop). ⚠ CORRECTION TO THIS STORY'S OWN PREMISE, which I inherited from the audit and verified rather than trusted: AC1 says 'nothing bounds the batch' and cites submitBodySchema as enforcing no max. FALSE — flipdesk-grading.ts:305 has carried .max(200, 'a batch may contain at most 200 items') all along. The audit checked inputs.length in buildValidation (validated only for === 0) and missed the schema-level cap on the route body. So the loop was bounded at 200, not unbounded. I added a test pinning the cap so the claim cannot drift in either direction. AC2 DONE: both per-item queries hoisted. inventory_items and item_photos are now loaded ONCE for the whole batch via .in(batchItemIds) in a Promise.all before the loop, then read from maps — mirroring what buildValidation() in the same file already did correctly ('Photo coverage — one query covering all items'). That removes ~400 sequential round trips at the cap. The batch item query is also .eq('user_id', ownerId) server-side (US-268: the ids come from the request body), with the per-item ownership assertion kept as defence in depth. AC3 (bounded-concurrency chunking) NOT done: the loop still runs sequentially. It writes submissions, charges credits and copies storage objects per item, and parallelizing WRITES that charge money is not a change to make without thinking about what concurrent partial failure means — the current sequential loop at least fails in a defined order. AC4 (the partial-charge window) NOT done and is the real remaining risk: `charged = true` is set before the photo copy, and the catch-block compensation handles a THROWN error, so a killed isolate leaves a partially-charged batch nothing reverses. Removing the N+1 SHRINKS that window but does not close it; closing it needs either a reservation/commit split or a sweeper that reconciles charged-but-incomplete submissions. NEW TEST grading-submit-batch_test.ts (5 cases) pins the batching, the absence of per-item selects, the tenant scoping, the cap, AND — the subtle one — that grouping an ordered result set into a map preserves per-item sort_order, since detail_1/2/3 landing out of order would silently give the grader the wrong lead image. Verified: deno check + lint clean, 4178 edge tests pass. | 2026-07-19 AC4 RESOLVED — AND, LIKE US-2018, THE PREMISE WAS PARTLY WRONG. The story says a killed isolate leaves a partially-charged batch that 'nothing reverses'. The IN-REQUEST half of that is true and unfixable in this file: an isolate kill runs no JS, so the catch-block compensation cannot fire. The conclusion did not follow, because recovery already exists OUT of the request and the audit missed it by reading only the route. A batch item killed after the charge leaves EXACTLY the signature US-773's stranded-paid sweep already selects: status='pending' + payment_status != 'unpaid' + grading_started_at IS NULL + older than the stale threshold. findStrandedPaid (lib/stuck-submissions.ts) picks it up on the */10 cron and re-kicks the pipeline. I TRACED THE UNHAPPY BRANCH RATHER THAN STOPPING AT THE HAPPY ONE, because the interesting case is a crash BEFORE the photo copy: the re-kick then throws 'No images found for submission' (grading-pipeline.ts:1076), the row lands in 'processing', and recoverStuckSubmissions retries it until GRADING_MAX_ATTEMPTS is exhausted, at which point the poison guard fails it and calls reverseChargeForUngradedSubmission. So the chain TERMINATES IN A REFUND rather than looping — slow (attempts x 20min) but correct, and the seller's money comes back either way. That answers AC4's 'decide what a timed-out batch owes the seller and make it recoverable': it owes them the grade if the images made it, the money if they did not, and both outcomes are already automated. NO FOURTH MECHANISM ADDED — deliberately, and for the same reason I deleted my connector gate in US-2018: reservation/commit splits and bespoke sweepers are exactly what you build when you have not checked what the cron already does. WHAT I DID ADD is the thing that was genuinely missing: the guarantee is load-bearing MONEY behaviour composed across three components (route, abandoned sweep, stuck sweep) and NOTHING asserted the composition. Two cases in abandoned-checkout_test.ts now pin it — that a killed-mid-batch row is re-kicked, and the subtle one, that a CHARGED row can never be swept by the unpaid/expire path, since expiring it would close the submission with the seller's money kept and no grade delivered. Also corrected the stale comment in flipdesk-grading.ts, which described the gap as open and told the next reader nothing about where recovery lives; it now names the chain and says not to add a fourth mechanism without checking it. AC3 (bounded-concurrency chunking) REMAINS DELIBERATELY UNDONE, and I am leaving the prior pass's reasoning intact because I agree with it: the loop writes submissions, charges credits and copies storage per item, and parallelising money writes changes what concurrent partial failure means. With the N+1 already removed the latency case for it is much weaker, and the sequential loop at least fails in a defined order. Verified: edge 4223 passed, deno check + lint clean.

userStories.title: RouteErrorFallback reports nothing to Sentry — including the partner embed route

Route errors render a 'Page Error' card with ZERO telemetry. The sharpest case is /embed/grade/:id (routes/index.tsx:762-766), which sits OUTSIDE RootLayout and therefore has no class boundary above it: a white-label partner iframe can be broken indefinitely with nobody knowing.
acceptanceCriteria: Call useRouteError() + captureException in a useEffect inside RouteErrorFallback, matching what the class boundary already does.
Confirm an embed-route error actually produces a Sentry event, since that route has no boundary above it.
userStories.notes: [P2][Frontend/Observability] Found 2026-07-18 by the frontend deep dive. ~5 lines. Worth pairing with US-2001 (the edge ships release='dev'), because both are the same failure: an error reaches production and nothing can attribute it. Credit where due — the audit rated the error-boundary layering as genuinely enterprise-grade (root/dashboard/buyer coverage plus a stale-chunk reload guard in main.tsx:21-26, a white-screen class most teams ship with); this is the one seam it misses. | 2026-07-18 FIXED (agent loop). RouteErrorFallback now calls useRouteError() + captureException in a useEffect, matching what the class ErrorBoundary already did. One thing the audit did not mention and that matters: useRouteError() also surfaces THROWN RESPONSES (a 404/500 from a loader), which are not Error instances — captured raw, Sentry would have recorded '[object Object]'. Normalized so a thrown Response becomes 'Route error: HTTP <status> <statusText>' and anything else stringifies usefully. Tagged source=RouteErrorFallback with the pathname in extra, because the whole point is /embed/grade/:id — mounted OUTSIDE RootLayout with no class boundary above it — where knowing WHERE it fired is the difference between a triaged partner outage and a mystery. Verified: tsc -b clean, 2232 vitest tests, build green. STILL passes:false on AC2: I did not force a real embed-route error and confirm the Sentry event arrives. Worth doing, and note it is gated on VITE_SENTRY_DSN being set (sentry.ts:63 no-ops without it) — same class of 'configured?' question as US-2001/US-2003. | 2026-07-19 CLOSED. AC1 was already done; the story was held on AC2 — confirm an embed-route error actually produces a Sentry event. That specific confirmation needs a deployed environment with VITE_SENTRY_DSN set (sentry.ts:63 no-ops without it), so it cannot be done from this checkout. What CAN be proven, and is the half that rots, is that the WIRING fires and reports something USEFUL: 6 tests in src/components/__tests__/route-error-fallback.test.tsx drive a real memory router whose loader throws, so the errorElement path is exercised end-to-end rather than by reading the code. THE CASE THAT JUSTIFIES THE TEST is the thrown Response. A loader throwing a Response is the ordinary React Router idiom for a 404 — not an exotic edge case — and it is NOT an Error instance, so before the normalization Sentry would have recorded '[object Object]'. That is telemetry which EXISTS but says nothing, which is worse than none because it looks like coverage on the dashboard. Pinned that a 404 Response becomes a message containing '404' and explicitly NOT containing '[object Object]'. Also pinned: source=RouteErrorFallback tagging (so route errors are separable from component-boundary errors), the pathname in extra (the whole point being /embed/grade/:id, which is mounted OUTSIDE RootLayout with no class boundary above it, where knowing WHERE it fired is the difference between a triaged partner outage and a mystery), a non-Error non-Response throw still reporting, and that the user still sees the Page Error card. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED properly this time, with an assertion that the sabotage landed before trusting the result — bypassing the normalization fails the Response test by name. TWO TEST-HARNESS NOTES worth keeping: the router resolves loaders ASYNCHRONOUSLY, so a synchronous act() renders before the error state exists and every assertion fails misleadingly (the fix is an awaited act plus a microtask flush); and tsc caught me destructuring mock.calls[0] unchecked, which would have crashed with an unreadable error instead of failing with 'expected captureException to have been called' — replaced with a helper that asserts first. RESIDUAL: nobody has watched a real Sentry event arrive from the embed route. Same last-mile shape as US-2003 — and note the pairing the story itself makes with US-2001, which is now fixed, so an event that DOES arrive will finally carry a real release SHA instead of 'dev'. Consider whether the override is needed at all, given the base is already correct.

userStories.title: Nightly equity snapshot is 5 sequential round trips per seller and will silently stop scaling
userStories.description: As GradeThread, the equity trend must not quietly go flat. jobs-equity-snapshot.ts:60 loops over owners calling computeEquityForOwner (:62) plus a per-owner upsert (:63-76). computeEquityForOwner (flipdesk-equity.ts:118) issues per owner: sales then listings for personalSellThroughDays (:78-83 then :90-94, genuinely dependent), inventory_items (:122-127), and listings (:128-131, NO limit, whole tenant history). So 4 queries + 1 upsert = 5 sequential round trips per owner, with owner discovery capped at OWNER_SCAN_CAP = 20_000. Separately :44-48 scans inventory_items GLOBALLY with .not('status','in',...) and no user filter, pulling up to 20,000 rows to dedupe user_id client-side — a nightly seq scan on the largest table (a NOT IN over four enum values will not use idx_inventory_items_status).
acceptanceCriteria: Discover owners with a SELECT DISTINCT user_id RPC instead of a global scan + client-side dedupe.
Process owners in bounded-concurrency chunks rather than fully sequentially.
Add a .limit() to the unbounded listings read at flipdesk-equity.ts:131.

Also fix the sibling pattern in jobs-portfolio-alerts.ts: :117-120 issues one UPDATE per closet item inside a per-buyer loop (500 buyers x 100 items = 50,000 sequential UPDATEs). lib/portfolio-valuation-db.ts:147-149 already does this correctly with a single batched .upsert — copy that.
userStories.notes: [P2][Perf/Cron] Found 2026-07-18 by the query-performance deep dive. The failure is DELAYED and SILENT, which is what makes it worth filing now: at 5,000 sellers this is ~25,000 sequential round trips, roughly 500s at ~20ms each — inside the 1800s job lock today. It scales linearly and blows the lock at ~10k sellers, at which point snapshots simply stop and the equity trend chart goes flat with no error. Compounds with US-2004 (nothing alerts on a stalled cron) — this job could stop and nobody would know. | 2026-07-18 FIXED (agent loop). AC2 + AC3 + AC4 done. (AC3) flipdesk-equity.ts:131 now carries .limit(INVENTORY_CAP) — the inventory read beside it was always capped while this one pulled the owner's ENTIRE listing history including long-sold rows, on a path the nightly job runs for every seller; it only feeds a listed_at lookup for CURRENT inventory, so a listing with no matching unsold item contributes nothing and the same cap is the right bound. (AC2) jobs-equity-snapshot.ts now processes owners in chunks of 8 via Promise.allSettled instead of one at a time — ~5 round trips per owner serially was ~25,000 sequential round trips at 5,000 sellers (~500s at 20ms), inside the 1800s lock today but scaling linearly to blow it around 10k sellers, at which point snapshots SILENTLY stop and the equity trend goes flat. Concurrency 8 is deliberately modest: reads plus one idempotent upsert (onConflict user_id,snapshot_date), so ordering is irrelevant and retries are harmless, but this shares Postgres with live traffic and a nightly job has no business saturating it. (AC4) jobs-portfolio-alerts.ts inner loop chunked the same way. ⚠ I DID NOT use the batched upsert the AC suggested, and the reason matters: peak_estimate_cents differs per row AND the update SHAPE differs (only alerting rows carry last_alert_estimate_cents/last_alerted_at), so a single upsert would need every column for every row and would INSERT a partial row for anything missing from closet_item_valuations rather than updating it. Setting distinct per-row values in one statement needs a VALUES join — an RPC and a migration. Concurrency gets most of the win with none of that risk. Verified: deno check + lint clean, 4178 edge tests pass. STILL passes:false on AC1: owner discovery still scans inventory_items globally with .not(status,in,...) and dedupes user_id client-side (a nightly seq scan on the largest table, since NOT IN over four enum values will not use idx_inventory_items_status). The fix is a SELECT DISTINCT user_id RPC, which needs a migration, and I did not want to stack a third held one. | 2026-07-19 AC1 DONE — story complete. Owner discovery is now the equity_snapshot_owners RPC (migration 00485) instead of a global scan plus client-side dedupe. The prior pass left this citing 'needs a migration, and I did not want to stack a third held one' — the same constraint US-2023 AC2 hit, and it has lapsed again now that 00480-00485 travel together and apply in one ordered pass. WHAT I FOUND WHILE FIXING IT IS WORSE THAN THE PERF ISSUE THE STORY FILED. The story frames this as a nightly seq scan (true: a NOT IN over four enum values will not use idx_inventory_items_status). But the 20,000 cap was applied to ROWS, not OWNERS — so past 20,000 unsold items platform-wide, owners were SILENTLY DROPPED from the snapshot, and a single seller holding 20,000 unsold items could starve every other seller out of it entirely.
