userStories.title: Certificate sitemap silently caps at ~1,000 — certUrls() never follows next_cursor
userStories.description: functions/_shared/sitemap.ts:52 declares next_cursor: string | null on CertSitemap, and certUrls() (:185-198) never reads it. The upstream /api/content/public/certificates.json defaults to limit=1000 (content-public.ts:1202), so only the most recent ~1,000 certificates (fewer after withheld filtering) ever reach /sitemap.xml or /sitemap-certs.xml. Certificates are the designated growth flywheel and the highest-volume indexable asset class we own — it stops scaling at 1k with no error and no log line.
acceptanceCriteria: certUrls() paginates via next_cursor until exhausted or a sane hard cap is hit.
If a hard cap is hit, split across numbered sub-sitemaps rather than truncating (SITEMAP_MAX_URLS is 5000, well under the 50k spec limit).
A test asserts that a mocked multi-page cursor response yields URLs from every page.
Confirm no other *Urls() generator in sitemap.ts has the same unread-cursor bug.
userStories.notes: [P1][SEO] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. Verified directly: the field is declared at :52 and referenced nowhere. Blocked-by-nothing, contained fix. Note US-1945 (public /cert/:id 404s in production) must also be resolved or the sitemap will simply advertise 404s at scale.

userStories.title: Sitemap serves 200 OK with whole sections silently dropped on upstream failure
userStories.description: fetchEdgeJson (functions/_shared/sitemap.ts:78-90) returns null on any error and each *Urls() generator then returns [], so a transient edge failure produces a structurally valid sitemap that is missing entire URL classes — served 200 and cached for an hour. Worse, a dropped section can push the total back under SITEMAP_MAX_URLS (sitemap.xml.ts:44-46), flipping /sitemap.xml from a sitemapindex to a truncated single urlset. functions/rss.xml.ts:24-33 was already hardened against exactly this failure mode (UpstreamUnavailable, US-2044); the sitemap never received the same treatment.
acceptanceCriteria: Port the rss.xml.ts UpstreamUnavailable pattern: on upstream failure serve 503 + Retry-After rather than a silently-incomplete 200.
Never let an upstream failure change the sitemapindex/urlset shape decision.
Emit a log line naming the section that failed.
Test: a failing generator produces 503, not a 200 missing that section.
userStories.notes: [P1][SEO] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. Telling a crawler a URL class no longer exists is worse than a 503 — it invites deindexing. | 2026-07-19 ALL FOUR ACs DONE. Ported the rss.xml.ts UpstreamUnavailable pattern (US-2044) that this story correctly identified as the fix already sitting in the codebase. fetchEdgeJson now THROWS instead of returning null, because returning null made 'the upstream is unreachable' indistinguishable from 'this section is legitimately empty' — and the generators' [] fallback turned that ambiguity into a structurally valid sitemap missing whole URL classes, served 200 and cached for an hour. Telling a crawler a page does not exist is a much more expensive lie than telling it to come back later. AC1 + AC2: /sitemap.xml catches and serves 503 + Retry-After, so an upstream blip can no longer change the sitemapindex-vs-urlset SHAPE decision either (a dropped section could push the total back under SITEMAP_MAX_URLS and silently collapse the index into a truncated single urlset). AC3: every failure path logs the route and the reason. AC4: a test asserts a failing generator yields 503 rather than a 200 missing that section. ⚠ THE SCOPE WAS BIGGER THAN THE STORY STATED, and finding that out was the point of checking: there are ELEVEN sub-sitemap routes and ALL of them had the identical exposure. Fixing only /sitemap.xml would have left ten routes silently truncating — and, worse, once fetchEdgeJson throws they would have started returning bare 500s instead. So they all had to move together. Ten now delegate to a shared sitemapResponse() helper rather than carrying ten copies of the same try/catch: the failure being guarded against is precisely the kind that gets fixed in one file and left in the rest. THE ELEVENTH IS THE INTERESTING ONE: sitemap-images.xml.ts could NOT use the shared wrapper because it serialises a different entry shape (imageSitemapXml, not urlsetXml). My bulk rewrite reported it as UNMATCHED rather than silently skipping it — which is exactly the file that would otherwise have been missed — and it now carries its own guard, with a comment saying why it differs. A 404 deliberately still returns null rather than throwing: that is a REAL answer ('no such collection'), and treating it as an outage would take the whole sitemap down for a legitimately absent section. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by unguarding one route: the 'every sub-sitemap route is guarded' test names it and fails. Verified: functions tsc clean, eslint 0 errors, web 2298 passed, build green.

userStories.title: Empty data reports are presented as citable findings — /state-of-durability and /transparency
userStories.description: /state-of-durability renders a 'GradeThread, The State of Secondhand Durability... CC BY 4.0' citation block over a dataset that is empty: live /api/grading/public/durability-report returns brands 0, sufficient_cohorts 0, regrades 0, most_durable []. /transparency shows human_agreement_rate: null and an MAE of '0.00' derived from 17 reviews, which reads as fabricated-perfect rather than low-sample. The build-time seeding machinery (scripts/prerender.mjs:220-268) is excellent — there is simply nothing to seed yet. This is the only finding in the audit that can actively damage credibility rather than merely underperform.
acceptanceCriteria: Any report page whose dataset is below a publishable threshold either noindexes itself or replaces the citation block with an explicit 'findings pending' state.
Never render a derived statistic (MAE, agreement rate) without an adjacent n= sample size.
Suppress rather than render 0.00/null headline metrics.
Define the minimum-n threshold per report in one place, mirroring the MIN_INDEX_TOTAL_SAMPLE=8 precedent already used by the condition index.
userStories.notes: [P1][GEO/Trust] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. The condition index already does this correctly (suppresses below n=8, never fabricates) — this story extends that discipline to the three report pages. Related: US-1691 (State of Secondhand Condition report) is the story that eventually fills these with real data. [2026-07-19 DONE — all 4 ACs] AC4 first: src/lib/report-thresholds.ts holds MIN_QUALITY_REVIEWS=30 and MIN_DURABILITY_COHORTS=8 in ONE place, the latter mirroring the MIN_INDEX_TOTAL_SAMPLE=8 precedent the condition index already enforces (a test asserts that parity against the edge constant). hasSufficientSample treats null/undefined/NaN as INSUFFICIENT — not knowing the sample is not the same as having one, and publishing a statistic of unknown support is the exact failure. AC1: /state-of-durability now noindexes itself AND swaps the CC BY 4.0 citation block for an explicit Findings pending state when sufficient_cohorts < 8. Both driven by ONE flag, deliberately — a page that noindexes but still says cite this report still invites citation from anyone arriving by link, and one that drops the citation but stays indexed still advertises an empty report. A test asserts they share the decision. AC2/AC3: /transparency renders n = <count> expert reviews next to the accuracy figures, and withholds the three DERIVED rates (agreement, MAE, misread) below n=30 rather than rendering them with a caveat — a number on the page gets cited regardless of the caveat beside it. The reported failure was MAE 0.00 from 17 reviews; a test asserts the threshold still excludes 17. ⚠ THE HALF THAT ALMOST SHIPPED BROKEN, caught by checking the built HTML rather than trusting the test: react-helmet-async v3 renders NO server-side head, so the noindex I first added via <SEO> reached the live SPA and NOT crawlers — precisely backwards for a page we want out of the index. Verified dist/state-of-durability.html had no robots meta. Fixed by teaching src/prerender/head-builder.ts to emit noindex,follow for an unpublishable report, reading the SAME build-time seed the body renders from so head and body cannot disagree. It fails CLOSED (absent seed -> noindex). Confirmed in the built output: state-of-durability.html now carries noindex,follow while pricing.html keeps the full rich-result directive. Same SPA-only trap as US-2105 and US-2044.

userStories.title: /blog hub is hard-capped at 20 posts with no pagination — older posts orphaned
userStories.description: functions/blog/[[path]].ts:141 fetches /api/content/public/posts?limit=20 and renders them wholesale. Post 21 and older have no crawl path from the hub — they are reachable only from a tag page or the sitemap. Tag pages (:505-524) are likewise unpaginated. This caps the blog's crawlable surface permanently, regardless of how much content the engine produces.
acceptanceCriteria: Paginate /blog with crawlable <a href> links (not JS-only), e.g. /blog/page/2.
Paginate tag pages the same way.
Paginated pages self-canonical (do not canonical every page to /blog) and stay indexable.
Add paginated URLs to the sitemap.

Fix the tag-page metadata while in here: no lastmod (sitemap.ts:174-180), an off-convention em-dash title separator (:539) instead of ' | GradeThread', and a square logo_icon_512.png as ogImage on a summary_large_image card (:542), which crops badly in unfurls.
userStories.notes: [P1][SEO] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. Worth doing before the content engine is switched on (US-2104), otherwise volume accumulates into an uncrawlable tail. [2026-07-19 DONE — all 5 ACs] Needed a new capability first: /posts was CURSOR-only, and a cursor cannot address a page — /blog/page/3 must resolve without replaying pages 1-2. Added optional offset (via .range) plus a total count, with CURSOR WINNING when both are supplied so existing API consumers are untouched; the count is only computed on the offset path. AC1/AC2: /blog/page/N and /blog/tag/<t>/page/N render with real <a rel=prev/next href> links — JS-only pagination is invisible to the crawlers this exists for. Tag pages slice the full set the tag endpoint already returns, so no extra round trip. AC3: every page self-canonicals; canonicalising page N to /blog would tell engines pages 2+ are duplicates and drop the exact posts the pagination exposes. /blog/page/1 301s to /blog so the two are never duplicate URLs, and a page past the end 404s rather than indexing an empty listing. AC4: paginated hub URLs enter the sitemap. AC5: tag lastmod was ALREADY fixed by my US-2100 work. Title separator corrected from an em-dash to the site-wide | GradeThread. ⚠ MY TEST FOUND TWO INSTANCES THE AC DID NOT NAME: the blog HUB and the post-page hero FALLBACK also used the square logo_icon_512.png as ogImage on summary_large_image cards — same defect as the tag page, fixed together. ⚠ AND THEN THE SAME TEST WAS TOO BROAD: logo_icon_512.png is still CORRECT as Organization.logo in the JSON-LD, where schema.org wants a square mark. A blanket file-level assertion would have pushed me to break valid markup, so it is now scoped to ogImage lines only. Sixth prose-matching guard failure this session — the AC5 assertions initially matched my own comments documenting the OLD values. Comment-stripping is now applied in the test with a note explaining why.

userStories.title: lastmod is today() on every dynamic hub URL and every sitemap-index entry
userStories.description: ROUTE_LAST_MODIFIED (public-routes.ts:90+) enforces an explicit 'NEVER the build timestamp' contract for static routes (US-429). Dynamic generators ignore that discipline: /blog (sitemap.ts:163), /verified (:204), /authors (:225), /condition-index (:250), /value (:276) and /durability (:299) all emit today(), as does every entry in sitemapIndexXml (:334). So every sub-sitemap claims it changed today, every day — which trains crawlers to distrust lastmod site-wide and undoes the benefit US-429 bought.
acceptanceCriteria: Derive each hub's lastmod from the newest child item's updated_at.
Derive each sitemap-index entry's lastmod from the newest URL inside that sub-sitemap.
Blog tag URLs get a real lastmod (currently none).
A test asserts no generator emits today() unconditionally.
userStories.notes: [P2][SEO] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. Cheap, and it protects a signal we already invested in for static routes. [2026-07-19 DONE — all 4 ACs] AC1: withHubLastmod() gives each hub its NEWEST CHILD date. Applied to the six hub generators (blog, sellers, authors, condition-index, value, durability). Deliberately NOT applied to certUrls/passportUrls — those are FLAT lists where element 0 is a real certificate, so hub-rewriting would corrupt its date with an unrelated sibling. A test asserts that exclusion so a later tidy-up cannot apply it uniformly. AC2: sitemapIndexXml now takes SitemapIndexEntry (string | {name,lastmod}); sitemap.xml.ts passes newestLastmod() of the URLs it already built for each section. sitemap-images.xml derives from the blog payload it is generated from. The payload gives tags as a flat string[] with no post mapping, so a per-tag date is not derivable — the newest published post is the honest UPPER BOUND (a tag page cannot have changed more recently than the newest post). Explicitly not today(), which is the lie being removed. AC4: the guard encodes the real intent rather than counting today(). Hub initializers still write today() and that is CORRECT — withHubLastmod overwrites it when children exist and keeps it only for a genuinely empty hub, where inventing an older date would be a different lie. So the assertion is: any generator writing lastmod: today() must also route through withHubLastmod (partitionedStaticUrls exempted and documented — its today() is the no-manifest home fallback). Negative-verified by reverting one generator to a bare return. ⚠ MY FIRST AC4 GUARD COUNTED 20 today() USES BECAUSE IT MATCHED MY OWN EXPLANATORY COMMENTS — the fifth prose-matching guard failure this session. Verified rather than assumed.

THE TEST IS THE PART WORTH READING: the first version listed five builders by hand, and when I reintroduced an anonymous node to check it, IT PASSED — none of the five happened to contain a fixed site. Rewrote it to DERIVE its coverage from every zero-arg *JsonLd export plus every FLIPDESK_LANDINGS entry (53 assertions), so a new builder is covered the day it is added. userStories.notes: [P2][Content] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. GATED: the domain is new and pSEO volume is already an indexability risk (vault/40-growth/seo-indexability.md) — do not start until the GSC Page-indexing diagnosis (US-2095) is read. Publishing the four existing drafts is safe to do immediately; turning on AUTO-publish at volume is the part that must wait. Prereqs overlap US-1566 (crons/SES) — coordinate. | 2026-07-19 AC3 DONE; AC1/AC2/AC4/AC5 UNTOUCHED and correctly gated (they need the GSC diagnosis US-2095, Coolify crons and a pacing decision — ops actions, not code). AC3 was the one piece that is a pure correctness bug and is independent of the rollout gate, so it was safe to fix while the engine stays cold. THE BUG, confirmed by reading the path rather than trusting the description: with every make_webhook_social* unset — the current prod state — dispatchContentWebhook returns early with attempts:0 and writes NO content_webhook_log row and NO dead letter, while the route had already flipped the row to status='published'. Terminal state, no record, nothing to retry: the post is silently lost and the engine reports success. I ALSO FOUND THE SAME HOLE IN THE SCHEDULER TICK (content-scheduler.ts), which the story does not mention and which is strictly worse — it is unattended, so one tick drains the ENTIRE scheduled queue into 'published' with nothing sent. Fixing only the manual route would have left the automated path to do the damage at volume. DELIBERATELY DID NOT IMPLEMENT AC3 AS WRITTEN. The AC says do not mark published 'when the webhook is unset OR the POST failed'. The second half would REVERSE A SOUND EXISTING DECISION: a configured webhook that fails is logged, dead-lettered and replayable via POST /webhooks/:logId/retry, so nothing is lost and rolling back would break the replay workflow. The two cases only look alike — one is recoverable and recorded, the other is neither. So the guard checks CONFIGURATION, not DELIVERY. Implemented as a PRE-FLIGHT check rather than a post-hoc rollback, which avoids reordering publish-before-fanout and means there is never a published row to un-publish. Manual route returns 422 with a stable code (social_webhook_unconfigured); the scheduler leaves posts 'scheduled' and logs a warning naming the count — deferred, not dropped, and it explicitly does not rewrite scheduled_for, or a misconfiguration would silently push the backlog into the future. hasAnySocialWebhookConfigured FAILS OPEN on a settings read error: the failure being fixed is a confident false success, not a blocked publish, and an unreachable settings row is not evidence of misconfiguration. 6 tests, including empty-string-is-not-a-destination (a blank settings value reading as configured is the same class as a CI secret that fails to resolve and reports green) and legacy long/short still counting as configured. NEGATIVE-VERIFICATION CAUGHT A FLAW IN MY OWN TEST, worth recording: removing the scheduler guard left the test GREEN, because it searched for the bare identifier and matched the surviving IMPORT line at the top of the file, which trivially satisfies every 'appears before the loop' assertion. Retargeted at the call expression; the removal now reddens it. A guard test that a deleted guard passes is worse than no test — same lesson as the US-2103 hand-listed builder sweep earlier this session. Verified: 4437 edge tests pass, deno check + lint clean.

State what can be said about the model and evaluation without leaking prompt IP.
Render tier data and flaw->factor->impact as real <table> elements — /condition-grading currently uses div cards, and tables are the structure most often lifted verbatim into LLM answers.
Coordinate with the grading-engine skill contract before changing any published criterion.
userStories.notes: [P2][GEO/Authority] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. This is the explicit PSA-playbook gap in the strategy doc's own mapping table, and it is the difference between 'a rubric' and 'the standard'. Adds no new URLs. [2026-07-19 PARTIAL — AC2+AC4 DONE, AC1 SUBSTANTIALLY DONE, AC3+AC5 OPEN] KEY FINDING: the premise was half wrong. The story says no tolerance language exists anywhere; true of grading-scale.ts/grade-standard.ts, but defect-weighting.ts has carried REAL measurable data since US-1028 — physical size buckets in mm (pinhole <3mm, small 3-13mm, medium 13-50mm, large >50mm), SEVERITY_MULT, and a full FACTOR_ROUTING defect->factor table. We were not missing the measurable standard, we were failing to PUBLISH it. Nothing had to be invented. Done: AC2 the 0.75 review threshold is stated explicitly on /grading/methodology via a guarded constant (grading-threshold-parity.test.ts fails if it diverges from the edge fallback); AC4 tier data is now a real <table> with scope/caption, and three new spec tables render the mm tolerances, severity multipliers and flaw->factor routing. New src/lib/grading-standard.ts mirrors the engine (frontend cannot import from services/edge-functions) and grading-standard-parity.test.ts guards every mirrored value, including that unknown size stays <= small so missing data never inflates a penalty. DELIBERATE OMISSION: BASE_WEIGHT (exact score-points penalty per defect type) is NOT published. Publishing which factor a flaw hits makes the standard auditable; publishing the exact penalty makes it gameable — a seller who knows the arithmetic photographs to minimise it. A test asserts it stays out. Reversing that is a product call. STILL OPEN: AC1 residue — pilling density and fade delta-E have NO engine equivalent and were deliberately not invented; adding them means defining new measurement in the engine first. AC3 (name the base model + eval numbers without leaking prompt IP) is unstarted and overlaps the US-2035 determinism decision. AC5 requires grading-engine skill/vault coordination since this now publishes engine criteria. | 2026-07-19 AC5 DONE. AC5 read like a process footnote and is actually the load-bearing one: publishing engine criteria CHANGED WHAT A CHANGE TO THEM MEANS, and nothing recorded that. SIZE_BUCKETS, SEVERITY_MULT and FACTOR_ROUTING went public on /condition-grading, but defect-weighting.ts — the file someone actually opens to tune grading — said nothing about it, and neither did the vault. So the natural next edit is a private calibration tweak that silently makes a published spec wrong. Fixed at the point of edit AND in the contract: a header warning on defect-weighting.ts naming exactly which three tables are mirrored and why that matters (the page exists to be cited and lifted verbatim into LLM answers, so a stale mirror is a precise, checkable, WRONG claim — worse than the adjectives it replaced), plus a new 'Published criteria' section in vault/20-domain/grading-scale-and-weights.md with defect-weighting.ts and grading-standard.ts added to code_refs so the CI drift guard now watches them. THE NON-OBVIOUS FACT, and I VERIFIED IT RATHER THAN ASSUMING: the parity guard lives in the WEB project, so `deno test` alone does NOT catch an engine-side change. Proved it by moving SEVERITY_MULT.minor 0.5 -> 0.6 with the mirror untouched — the edge suite passed 18/18 completely happily while the web guard failed on 'severity multipliers match SEVERITY_MULT'. An engine developer running the obvious local suite would have shipped it. That is now called out in both the source warning and the note, with the instruction to run npm run verify. Also carried the BASE_WEIGHT omission into both places as a PRODUCT TRADE-OFF rather than an unfinished edge — auditable vs gameable — because 'the published standard is missing the penalties' reads like a completeness bug to anyone who has not seen the argument. STILL OPEN: AC1 residue (pilling density, fade delta-E have no engine equivalent; adding them means defining new measurement in the engine first, not writing prose) and AC3 (naming the base model + eval numbers), which remains blocked behind the US-2035 determinism product decision. Verified: 2472 web + 4437 edge tests pass, deno check + lint clean, vault:lint clean at 100 notes.

userStories.title: Viral-loop attribution leaks and a blank certificate OG fallback
userStories.description: The certificate share loop is the designated organic acquisition flywheel, and it leaks at three points: buyer-to-buyer re-shares carry no ref= because the code gates on !!user (src/components/.../cert-share-actions.tsx:54), so the highest-reach shares are unattributed; the SSR cert CTA drops attribution entirely (functions/cert/[id].ts:249); and the cert OG image falls back to a transparent 1x1 PNG on edge failure (functions/og/cert/[id].ts:24), cached 300s — a blank link preview, which is worse for CTR than a branded fallback.
acceptanceCriteria: Attach a referral/attribution parameter to every cert share path, including anonymous re-shares.
Preserve attribution through the SSR CTA.
Replace the 1x1 transparent fallback with a branded static OG image.
Mount the PWA install prompt somewhere with real install intent — it is currently only on flipdesk/intake.tsx:489 and snap.tsx:80, not the dashboard or landing.
userStories.notes: [P2][Growth] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. Depends on US-1945 (cert pages 404 in prod) being fixed first — the loop is dead until then. | 2026-07-19 AC1+AC3 DONE; AC2 DELIBERATELY NOT DONE (argued below); AC4 untouched. First, the stated DEPENDENCY IS STALE: US-1945 says cert pages 404 in prod, but its own latest note records the certificate it names still returning HTTP 200 live — what is actually missing is the homepage sample-cert link (an unset Pages env var). Cert pages resolve, so the share loop is not dead and this was workable. AC1: attribution was built as one refSuffix that appeared ONLY when the viewer had a referral code, which coupled two different things. ref= is a CLAIM ON A CREDIT and needs someone to credit; utm_* is a DESCRIPTION OF A PATH and is true regardless. Split them: every share now carries utm_source/medium/campaign (cert_referral vs cert_organic, so the two halves of the loop can be measured separately) plus per-channel utm_content, while ref= still appears only for a sharer who actually has a code. EXPLICITLY DID NOT make anonymous re-shares inherit the ref the visitor arrived with — that is the tempting version of this fix and it would credit a seller for a stranger's audience, inventing an earning event while looking like closing an attribution gap. Pinned by a test that fails if an anonymous share ever carries a ref. AC3: the 1x1 transparent fallback is not just the cert — it is the SAME defect in all five og/* endpoints (cert, blog, verified, grade-check, social/card), so I fixed the class via a shared brandedFallbackResponse() that streams the existing static /og-image.png and drops to the pixel only if that is also unreachable. Deliberately NOT applied to badge/* and slab/*: those have their own dimensions, and an invisible badge degrades better than a wrong-shaped brand card stretched into a badge slot. Fallback TTL stays 300s against the real card's 24h, because this response means upstream was unavailable — caching a generic card for a day at a scraper we cannot purge would outlast the outage and permanently mis-image every share created in that window. Added an X-GT-Fallback header since a degraded card and a real one are otherwise both just a 200 with PNG bytes. AC2 IS THE INTERESTING ONE AND I DID NOT DO IT, because doing it as written is a correctness bug: the cert SSR response is SHARED-EDGE-CACHED on origin+pathname with the query string DROPPED (withEdgeCache in blog-render.ts), so varying the CTA href by the visitor's ?ref= would cache the first arriver's referral code and serve it to every later visitor of that certificate — one seller silently credited for everyone else's traffic, which is strictly worse than the leak. And there is almost nothing to preserve: /cert/:id renders under RootLayout, which calls captureAffiliateRef() on mount, so a JS-enabled visitor banks the ref before they can click the link; the gap is no-JS agents, which are overwhelmingly crawlers, and a crawler does not sign up. Reasoning left as a comment at the CTA so the next person does not 'fix' it into cache poisoning. This is the third audit claim this session that did not survive verification (cf. US-2030, US-2020). AC4 (PWA install prompt placement) not started — it is a UX placement decision, not a defect. Verified: 2472 web tests pass, tsc -b + functions tsconfig clean, negative-verified both the pre-fix coupling and the borrow-a-ref variant. | 2026-07-22 AC4 DONE (agent loop). The prior note left AC4 as an untaken UX placement decision, but the AC itself names the surfaces ('not the dashboard or landing'), so this is an implementation, not a fresh decision: mounted <PwaInstallBanner variant="general"/> on src/pages/dashboard.tsx (right under the PageHeader). The banner is inert unless the browser fires beforeinstallprompt AND the user has not dismissed it, and it shares ONE dismiss key across all mounts (intake/snap/dashboard), so adding a third surface never nags — it just reaches an engaged, returning user (the highest real install intent) instead of only the FlipDesk-intake/Snap paths. general variant copy is grades/certificates-oriented, correct for the consumer dashboard. Verified: tsc -b + eslint clean. STILL passes:false on AC2 ALONE, which is a documented CORRECTNESS refusal, not an oversight: the cert SSR response is shared-edge-cached on origin+pathname with the query string dropped (withEdgeCache), so varying the CTA href by the visitor ?ref= would cache the first arriver's referral code and serve it to everyone — AC2 as written is a cache-poisoning bug. Closing it needs a non-query-string mechanism (e.g. client-side capture after navigation), which is genuine remaining work. AC1 (split utm_* channel vs ref= credit, incl. anonymous shares) + AC3 (shared brandedFallbackResponse across all og/* endpoints) were already done.

userStories.title: No product/pricing/UI A/B testing — PostHog flags are never read client-side
userStories.description: There is a sophisticated server-side flag engine with deterministic FNV-1a bucketing, rollout percentages and plan targeting (lib/feature-flags.ts:114-166), plus four experiment engines (lib/experiments-governor.ts:19) — but they cover email subject lines, drip timing and AI prompts only. PostHog is initialized yet only capture() is ever called (src/lib/analytics.ts:237-239); feature flags are never read, there is no client useFeatureFlag hook and no exposure event. So paywall copy, pricing presentation and onboarding cannot currently be tested. All the primitives exist — this is a connector, not a framework build.
acceptanceCriteria: Add a client useFeatureFlag hook backed by PostHog, with an exposure event so results are analyzable.
Respect the existing consent gating — no flag evaluation before consent.
Prove it with one real experiment on a conversion surface (paywall copy or pricing layout).
Document how server-side flags and client-side experiments relate, so the two systems do not drift.
userStories.notes: [P2][Growth/Experimentation] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. Pairs with US-2101 (UTM capture) — together they make conversion work measurable rather than anecdotal. | 2026-07-19 AC1+AC2+AC4 DONE; AC3 (one real experiment) DELIBERATELY LEFT OPEN. The connector exists: src/lib/client-experiments.ts (logic, testable without React) + src/hooks/use-feature-flag.ts (subscription plumbing), returning {variant, ready}. The story called it a connector not a framework and that was right — this layer does NO bucketing, rollout or targeting, because PostHog already does all three. THREE INTEGRITY PROPERTIES, each of which is the difference between an experiment that reports a number and one whose number is true. (1) CONSENT IS STRUCTURAL, NOT CHECKED: flags are read off window.posthog, which analytics.ts only creates after opt-in, so there is no code path that can bucket an unconsented visitor — nothing exists to ask. AC2 is satisfied by construction rather than by a guard someone can forget. (2) NO MID-SESSION FLIPS: a resolved variant is LOCKED for the page session. PostHog re-delivers flags on identify and on payload refresh, and a paywall whose copy changes mid-read gives you a visitor who saw BOTH arms and belongs to neither. (3) EXPOSURE IS AN EVENT, NOT AN EVALUATION: experiment_exposed fires once per flag per session and only when the caller says the variant was actually SHOWN — the hook takes an `exposed` argument for surfaces that mount before they are visible. Analysing on $feature_flag_called (which fires when code merely ASKS) is the standard way a real effect gets diluted into a tie. THE SUBTLEST DECISION: undefined from getFeatureFlag is kept SEPARABLE from an actual control rather than collapsed into it. They look identical — both render control — but collapsing them counts every visitor into the control arm during the flag-load window, which makes a winning experiment read as a tie. That is why the return is {variant, ready} and not just a string. 13 tests. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED all three properties by simulating the careless edit: dropping the lock reddens 2, dropping the exposure resolution-guard reddens 1, collapsing undefined into control reddens 3; restoring returns to green. AC4 DONE as vault/40-growth/experimentation.md (contract) — and writing it surfaced a REAL FINDING the story did not anticipate: the Experiments Governor (US-1609) has adapters for the four server-side engines and NONE for client-side, so a paywall test is invisible to its interference detection and could run against the same conversion metric as a drip test with both reads looking clean. Recorded as a warning callout with the manual check to do meanwhile. Also noted: the consent category model has no vault note, which is a gap. AC3 NOT DONE ON PURPOSE: there is no web paywall component (paywall is iOS/Android), so the named surface is the pricing page, and choosing what to test there means authoring alternative pricing copy/layout — a product and design decision, not a code one. The mechanism is ready and wiring a chosen variant is now a small edit. Verified: 2462 web tests pass, tsc -b clean, vault:lint clean (3 drift warnings pre-existing from earlier commits today, not from this work).

userStories.description: functions/passport/[slug].ts SSRs passport pages with complete Product JSON-LD (json-ld.ts:699), and src/pages/passport.tsx passes jsonLd — but there is no passportUrls() in functions/_shared/sitemap.ts, unlike certs, sellers, authors, value and durability which all have one. The pages are discoverable only via inbound links. Note these sit outside the static-route CI guard, which skips any path containing ':' (public-routes.test.ts:42), so nothing flags the omission.
acceptanceCriteria: Add passportUrls() following the certUrls pattern (with cursor pagination done correctly per US-2096).
Wire it into the sitemap index.
Confirm the pages should be indexed at all — if they are user-owned surfaces like /trust/:handle, noindex them deliberately instead and document why.
userStories.notes: [P3][SEO] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. Decide indexability first; do not add URLs by default given the indexability constraint. [2026-07-19 DONE — all 3 ACs] AC3 FIRST, as the story demanded (decide indexability before adding URLs). ANSWERED BY EVIDENCE, not preference: functions/passport/[slug].ts states the intent outright — the marquee buyer-facing provenance surface, one INDEXABLE, AI-citable page per garment ... PII-free by construction. It carries no noindex, unlike /trust/:handle which is explicitly x-robots-tag noindex and private-by-default. So passports are meant to be indexed and the cited comparison surface is the counter-example, not the model. AC1: new GET /api/content/public/passports.json (cursor-paginated on created_at, limit capped at 5000) + passportUrls() in functions/_shared/sitemap.ts, written cursor-correct FROM THE START rather than repeating the US-2096 bug — non-advancing-cursor break and a 50k ceiling that logs rather than truncating silently. AC2: wired into the sitemap index (counts toward the index-vs-urlset threshold, listed in the sitemapindex) plus a new functions/sitemap-passports.xml.ts sub-route with the US-2097 503 guard. VISIBILITY GATE: public_passport_slug is the publish opt-in, and it is the SAME predicate GET /api/passport/:slug resolves against. That parity is what stops the sitemap advertising a URL that 404s or leaking an unpublished garment. Negative-verified by removing the .not(...is null) filter — the guard fails. Registered /sitemap-passports.xml in public/_routes.json; without it Cloudflare Pages serves a static 404 instead of invoking the Function, the same silent prod failure the US-424 guard caught on /llms-full.txt last commit. A test now asserts that entry directly. ⚠ OBSERVED, NOT CAUSED BY THIS WORK: the vitest suite is FLAKY under parallel load. Slow file-scanning guards (no-or-on-mutations, lockstep-registry, both ~8.6s) fail nondeterministically and the failing test varies run to run. Measured: with my changes stashed the clean tree produced 10 failures; with them applied, 1. All pass in isolation. Worth its own story — a suite that fails randomly trains people to re-run rather than investigate.

userStories.title: Image sitemap covers 8 of 213 routes via a hand-synced list; CF Transformations still off
userStories.description: functions/_shared/sitemap.ts:379-441 hardcodes 8 marketing images with a 'KEEP IN SYNC with ROUTE_OG_IMAGES' comment (:378) and no CI guard — Pages Functions cannot import from src/, and unlike llms.txt (which solved the identical cross-boundary problem by consuming the build-emitted dist/seo-manifest.json) this one was left manual. Separately, VITE_CF_IMAGE_RESIZING=false in .env.production (verified, :39) gates the entire srcset in responsive-image.tsx:32-33, so production ships full-size originals with no srcset/sizes on every public image.
acceptanceCriteria: Generate MARKETING_IMAGES from dist/seo-manifest.json, mirroring the llms.txt approach, or add a CI guard on the sync.
Enable Cloudflare Transformations on the zone, then flip VITE_CF_IMAGE_RESIZING — in that order.
Do not flip the flag first: responsive-image.tsx:27-31 documents that a failed srcset candidate does not fall back to src, so enabling it before the zone feature renders every image broken.
userStories.notes: [P3][SEO/Perf] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. width/height are already emitted so CLS is protected; the unrealized win is bytes/LCP. Blocked on a Cloudflare dashboard toggle, not code. | 2026-07-19 AC1 DONE; AC2/AC3 remain BLOCKED on a Cloudflare dashboard toggle (not code). The image sitemap no longer hand-syncs: vite.config.ts seoManifestPlugin emits a per-route `image` {file,alt} from ROUTE_OG_IMAGES into dist/seo-manifest.json, and functions/_shared/sitemap.ts marketingImageUrls derives from it — the same cross-boundary pattern llms.txt already used, which is what the story asked for. Verified parity: the derived set is EXACTLY the 8 the constant hardcoded, so this is a sourcing change with zero output diff today, and a new share card now arrives with no second edit. TWO JUDGEMENT CALLS WORTH RECORDING. (1) Only routes with a DISTINCT card are emitted, plus home (which legitimately represents itself with the site-wide default). Emitting the default for all 213 routes would have been the mechanical reading of "covers 8 of 213" and would have produced a sitemap repeating one image 200+ times — duplicate-image noise, not coverage. The 213 number in the story title describes ROUTES, not routes that should carry an image. (2) The old constant is KEPT as a fallback rather than deleted, because the manifest is fetched over the network at the edge and an empty image sitemap tells Google we removed every image we have; stale-but-correct beats empty. Its comment now says do-not-add-here. THE SUBTLE CASE, and the one that got a test: a manifest emitted by a build PREDATING the image field has zero image-bearing routes, which is indistinguishable from an intentional empty set unless you decide otherwise — read as "empty" it would blank the image sitemap on the first deploy after a rollback, so it falls back and logs instead. image:caption is now the ROUTE_OG_IMAGES alt verbatim (they were already identical strings) and image:title is the registry title, so both are derived rather than a third copy of the same prose. 4 tests: derived mapping + no-card routes excluded, a brand-new card the fallback has never heard of, manifest unreachable, and the image-less-manifest case. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by flipping the fallback condition to always-trust-the-manifest: 4 tests turn red, including both fallback paths. Verified: 2396 web tests pass, tsc -b clean, build emits 8 image routes.

userStories.title: Entry bundle at 61.91/64 KB gz with structural upward pressure from the route table
userStories.description: scripts/check-bundle-budget.mjs:51-52 enforces entry <=64 KB gz and eager graph <=215 KB gz. The header comments document steady growth — 48.2 -> 54.6 -> 57.0 -> 61.91 KB over roughly three weeks — attributed each time to route-table growth in src/routes/index.tsx. With ~2 KB of headroom and a ~250-route eager route table as the cause, this budget will be breached shortly, and the usual fix (raise the ceiling) trades away LCP on the marketing pages this whole audit is about.
acceptanceCriteria: Lazy-load or code-split the route table so adding a route does not grow the entry chunk linearly.
Re-measure and record the new baseline.
Do not simply raise the budget ceiling without a stated reason.
userStories.notes: [P3][Perf/CWV] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. Filed now because the cause is structural rather than incidental — it will fail on an unrelated PR and get raised reflexively under time pressure. | 2026-07-19 MEASURED + EARLY-WARNING ADDED; the structural fix (AC1) DELIBERATELY NOT ATTEMPTED. CURRENT STATE, measured: entry 62.44/64 KB gz (1.56 KB left), eager total 213.16/215 KB (1.84 KB left) — the story's prediction is essentially realised; the next route added breaches. WHAT IS ACTUALLY IN THE ENTRY, so nobody re-derives it: the eager app modules are only sonner, button, card, error-boundary, cookie-consent, root-layout and routes/index — all legitimately eager. The eager node_modules are lucide-react (15 icon modules), react-helmet-async (1) plus its three CommonJS shims react-fast-compare/invariant/shallowequal (2 each), zustand (2), and small radix/clsx/cva/tailwind-merge helpers. NO CHEAP WIN EXISTS THERE: the lucide icons belong to genuinely-eager components (the error boundary and cookie banner render before anything else), and Helmet is load-bearing for SPA-navigation title/meta updates. ⚠ I NEARLY FILED A FALSE FINDING and am recording it because it would have been expensive: an early grep suggested HelmetProvider appeared ONLY in a test file, which would have meant react-helmet-async plus 3 CJS shims were dead weight in the most size-constrained chunk in the app. That was a `head -3` TRUNCATION ARTIFACT — src/components/seo.test.tsx sorts before src/main.tsx, which DOES render HelmetProvider (main.tsx:48). Removing Helmet on that basis would have silently broken client-side head updates on every SPA navigation, on the SEO surface this whole audit is about. Verify before deleting; do not trust a truncated grep. WHAT I DID INSTEAD, and why it fits the AC's intent: check-bundle-budget.mjs now WARNS at <=3 KB headroom, NAMES the top eager node_modules in the chunk, and says explicitly not to raise the ceiling. The file's own history is four raises (48.2 → 54.6 → 57.0 → 61.91 → 62.44), each blaming route-table growth and each followed by 'the real fix remains overdue'. That pattern is not carelessness — it is what happens when a budget first speaks on the PR that HAPPENS to cross it, which is almost never the PR that caused the growth and is usually under time pressure. A warning that arrives WITH the cause attached, while there is still room to act, is the thing that breaks that loop. It never fails the build (verified: exit 0 with warnings printed) — a warning that can block is just a lower ceiling. AC1 (split the route table) REMAINS OPEN and is the real fix: 227 routes are already lazy() per page, so the weight is the route TABLE itself, and splitting it means React Router's patchRoutesOnNavigation / Fog of War — which interacts with the prerenderer, the PUBLIC_ROUTES SEO registry and 404 handling. That is a genuine refactor, not a tidy-up, and doing it blind at P3 with the SEO surface downstream is a bad trade. It now has a warning that will ask for it BY NAME before the ceiling gets raised again. URGENCY 2026-07-19: the /admin/authenticity route pushed the eager bundle to 213.52/215 KB gz — 1.48 KB of headroom left (entry 62.8/64). The budget check now reports NEAR LIMIT. The next route addition will likely breach it, and the guard text explicitly says not to raise the ceiling because the cause is the eager route table. DONE 2026-07-19: admin subtree split into src/routes/admin-routes.tsx as DESCENDANT routes under a /admin/* splat, so its 81 lazy declarations and 86 route objects load only when someone reaches /admin. MEASURED: entry 62.8 -> 57.0 KB gz, eager 213.52 -> 208.34 KB gz. The budget check moved from NEAR LIMIT (1.48 KB left) to OK with 6.66 KB of headroom. Route components were ALREADY lazy — the cost was the table itself (each lazy() declaration plus each route object ships in the entry chunk), which is why adding one admin page moved the needle at all. Extracted the custom lazy() wrapper and SuspenseWrapper into src/routes/lazy.tsx rather than duplicating them: a local copy in the new module would have silently dropped the stale-chunk reload recovery for every admin page, a regression that only surfaces on a deploy. TRADEOFF ACCEPTED: descendant routes do not participate in the data router (no loader/action for this subtree) — verified none were declared before the split. InShellNotFound is shared with the /dashboard/* 404 so its declaration stays in index.tsx and is re-declared in the admin module; both resolve to the same dynamic import, so Vite emits one chunk. 806 SEO/prerender guard tests pass, tsc + eslint clean, 213 pages prerender.

userStories.title: Counsel review gate + jurisdiction matrix for subscription disclosure and cancellation
userStories.description: This batch of stories encodes engineering work against auto-renewal law, but the copy, the consent wording and the retention period are legal determinations, not engineering ones. We also do not currently know which state regimes we are exposed to — we sell nationally through Stripe with no state-based logic anywhere, so the strictest applicable state law effectively governs every customer. Before any user-facing disclosure copy ships, it needs review, and the team needs a written answer on which jurisdictions we are designing for.
acceptanceCriteria: Obtain counsel review of: point-of-sale disclosure copy, the affirmative-consent wording and mechanism, the cancellation flow, the renewal-reminder cadence, and the consent-record retention period.

Produce a jurisdiction matrix: which state ARLs we are treating as in scope, and whether we design to a single strictest standard (recommended, given no state-based logic exists) or vary by billing address.

Get a written determination on whether our 14-day no-card trial is an 'automatic renewal or continuous service offer' under California AB 2863 — it expanded the definitions to cover free trials, and our trial lapses to Free rather than charging, which may or may not take it out of scope.
Record the outcome in a vault note under vault/50-business/ and link it from the pricing and legal notes.

Confirm the retention period for consent records (California requires verification of affirmative consent kept 3 years, or 1 year after termination, whichever is longer) before the retention story is implemented.
userStories.notes: [P0][Compliance/Legal] Found 2026-07-18 by the subscription-compliance deep-dive audit. LEGAL CONTEXT (verified 2026-07-18, not legal advice): the FTC's 2024 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED by the Eighth Circuit on 2025-07-08 and is not in force. The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. The binding obligations today are (a) ROSCA 15 U.S.C. 8403 and FTC Act Section 5, both actively enforced, and (b) STATE automatic-renewal laws — most importantly California's ARL as amended by AB 2863, effective 2025-07-01, which is stricter than what we do today and expressly covers free trials. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). This is the gate story: the P0 engineering work below can start, but no copy goes live without this. Do not let an agent invent legal language.

userStories.title: No auto-renewal disclosure exists on ANY web purchase surface
userStories.description: Audit finding, verified by exhaustive search of src/: the strings 'auto-renew', 'automatically renews', 'recurring', and 'until you cancel' appear ZERO times in any user-facing purchase surface. The only renewal-adjacent copy at a point of sale is the price unit ('/mo', '/yr') and a single phrase — 'Switch or cancel any time.' — in src/components/billing/flipdesk-plan-picker-dialog.tsx:111. Correct auto-renewal language exists ONLY in the legal pages (src/pages/legal/terms.tsx:69-71 'renew automatically until cancelled'; refund.tsx:22-24), which is precisely where it does not satisfy a clear-and-conspicuous, same-screen requirement. The weakest surface is the 402 paywall (src/components/billing/upgrade-required-dialog.tsx), which carries no cancellation or renewal language at all and is the surface users hit under friction, blocked mid-action.
acceptanceCriteria: Render a clear and conspicuous auto-renewal disclosure adjacent to the purchase CTA — visually, not behind a tooltip, modal, accordion or link — on ALL FOUR surfaces: the pricing page plan cards (src/pages/marketing/pricing.tsx), the plan picker (flipdesk-plan-picker-dialog.tsx), the 402 paywall (upgrade-required-dialog.tsx), and buyer billing (src/pages/buyer/billing.tsx:147-220).

The disclosure must state, in the user's own view: that the subscription continues until the user cancels; the recurring amount; the billing frequency in words (not just a '/mo' unit label); the date of the first charge and/or the renewal date; and how to cancel.
Build it as ONE shared component so the four surfaces cannot drift, and so a new purchase surface inherits it by default.
Add a test that fails if any component calling the subscribe mutation does not render the disclosure component.
Copy must come from the counsel review gate, not be drafted by an agent.

userStories.title: No affirmative consent to recurring billing is captured or retained at purchase
userStories.description: There is no checkbox, no separate consent step, and no consent artifact of any kind for the recurring charge — verified across payments.ts, billing.tsx and pricing.tsx (zero hits). Stripe's consent_collection parameter is not used on the Checkout Session (services/edge-functions/src/routes/payments.ts:395-422, 542-554), and no custom_text is set. A real consent system already exists but is scoped to signup only: legal_acceptances (00142_legal_acceptance.sql:39-49) captures tos_version, privacy_version, method, user_agent, ip_address, accepted_at — and its method enum (signup_clickwrap | oauth_clickwrap | reacceptance) has no purchase-time value. It is never written at subscribe time. Separately, the highest-volume path is the weakest evidence: the signup trigger insert (:121-126) omits ip_address and user_agent entirely.
acceptanceCriteria: Capture express affirmative consent to the recurring charge at purchase, separate from and in addition to general ToS acceptance.
Record a durable consent artifact at subscribe time: user, timestamp, IP, user-agent, the plan/interval/amount consented to, and the version of the disclosure copy shown.

Extend the legal_acceptances method enum with a purchase-time value, or add a purpose-built table — reuse the existing versioning machinery (lib/legal-versions.ts) rather than inventing a second system.
Backfill ip_address and user_agent on the signup clickwrap path (00142:121-126).
Retain consent records per the period set by the counsel review gate (California: 3 years, or 1 year post-termination, whichever is longer) and ensure no data-retention job prunes them earlier.
Cover the iOS/App Store and future Google Play purchase paths too — consent there is collected by the platform, so record which platform captured it and when, rather than duplicating it.

Today we could not demonstrate what any subscriber agreed to. Depends on the terms-snapshot story for the 'what was shown' half. | 2026-07-19 INVESTIGATED, NOT IMPLEMENTED — and the scoping matters, so here is what the next pass needs. THIS STORY IS GENUINELY MORE COUNSEL-GATED THAN ITS NEIGHBOURS. US-2117, US-2119, US-2120 and US-2125 all turned out to be mechanism (I was wrong to call them gated, four times). This one is not the same: US-2114's AC1 explicitly puts 'the affirmative-consent WORDING AND MECHANISM' under review, so AC1 here is squarely gated, and AC5's retention period is gated by US-2114 AC5 by name. AC4 IS NOT GATED, and I traced it to a precise conclusion. THE MECHANISM ALREADY EXISTS: POST /api/legal/accept (routes/legal.ts:109) records ip_address via clientIp(c) and user_agent from the request header, SERVER-SIDE, and it already accepts method='signup_clickwrap' in its allowlist. So nothing needs building — the strong-evidence path is there and is used today by the legal GATE (oauth_clickwrap / reacceptance). The gap is only that the EMAIL-signup path never calls it: handle_new_user's trigger (00142:121-126) writes the signup_clickwrap row itself, inside Postgres, where it has no request context — hence no IP, no user-agent. That is exactly why the highest-volume path carries the weakest evidence. ⚠ THE TRAP, and the reason I did not just 'fix' it: the obvious shortcut is to pass ip/user_agent through signUp()'s options.data so the trigger can read them. DO NOT. Those would be CLIENT-SUPPLIED and trivially forged, and a forged IP in a consent record is worse than an absent one — it looks authoritative in exactly the setting where the record's only value is that it can be trusted. Same reasoning as US-2117's refusal to write a partial agreement and US-2119's refusal to send a dateless notice. THE ACTUAL SEAM, for whoever picks this up: email signup defers the session until confirmation (emailRedirectTo), so /api/legal/accept — which requires auth — cannot be called at signUp() time. The right hook is the FIRST AUTHENTICATED SESSION, in use-auth.ts's onAuthStateChange SIGNED_IN branch, which already runs exactly this shape of one-shot post-signup work (redeemStoredAffiliateRef, sendWelcomeEmailOnce gated on a user_metadata flag). Call /api/legal/accept with method='signup_clickwrap' there. ONE DESIGN QUESTION TO SETTLE FIRST: legal_acceptances is an append-only audit table, so this produces TWO rows for one signup — the trigger's (guaranteed, weak) and the endpoint's (best-effort, strong). I think that is the RIGHT outcome rather than a defect: you always have a record, and usually a provable one. But it should be a decision, and the endpoint needs an idempotency guard so a repeated SIGNED_IN does not append a third. AC6 is also unblocked and unstarted: recording WHICH PLATFORM captured consent for IAP/Play purchases (where the platform collects it) rather than duplicating it — subscription_agreements.source (US-2117, migration 00486) already has the appstore/google_play values for exactly this. | 2026-07-19 (cont.) AC6 DONE. Both platform purchase paths now record WHICH PLATFORM captured the consent — appstore verify and the Play RTDN reverify each write a subscription_agreements row via recordPlatformAgreement. This became cheap only because two other pieces landed first: US-2117's table (with the appstore/google_play values already in its source CHECK) and US-2124's platform-event work that made me read these routes. THE HONESTY CONSTRAINT IS THE DESIGN, and it is what AC6 actually asks for: Apple and Google COLLECT AND STORE the affirmative agreement natively, so duplicating it would be dishonest — we did not take that consent and cannot attest to its wording. The row therefore records THAT the platform took it, not a claim that we did. Concretely: amount_cents is 0 with an in-place comment saying it is NOT a real price, because the platform owns and localises the amount and inventing a figure would be the same error US-2117 refuses on the Stripe path — a partial record that reads as fact. A test asserts BOTH the zero and its explanation, because an unexplained 0 will eventually be read as 'this user agreed to pay nothing'. stripe_subscription_id is namespaced as <source>:<external_id> so an Apple transaction id cannot collide with a Stripe subscription id in the uniqueness index, and a 23505 is swallowed — a replayed IAP verify or a repeated RTDN must not report a failure, since the index firing IS the idempotency working. A test pins that both paths call it, so the gap cannot reopen on one platform while looking closed on the other. WHAT THIS CHANGES IN PRACTICE: before, 'what did this user agree to?' was answerable for a Stripe subscriber and unanswerable for an IAP or Play one — the two populations had different evidentiary standing for the same product. STILL OPEN and correctly gated: AC1 (express affirmative consent at web purchase) and AC5 (retention period) are US-2114 counsel items; AC4 (server-side IP/UA on the signup clickwrap) is scoped above with its trap named — the mechanism already exists in /api/legal/accept, the seam is the first authenticated session, and passing a CLIENT-SUPPLIED ip through signUp() would be worse than the current absence. Verified: edge 4319 passed, deno check + lint clean.

userStories.title: No record of what price or terms any user actually agreed to — pricing_plans is mutated in place
userStories.description: The users table stores flipdesk_plan and flipdesk_interval but NO amount column; price is resolved live on every read via getFlipdeskPriceIds() against pricing_plans. pricing_plans (00166:69-80) is mutated in place with only an updated_at trigger — no history table, no versioning. flipdesk_subscription_events records from_plan/to_plan and the raw payload but, per the note already in 00215_revenue_dashboard.sql:20, not even the billing interval. Combined, there is no way to reconstruct what price any user was shown or agreed to on any past date. If a price changes, the historical record changes with it.
acceptanceCriteria: Snapshot the agreed terms onto the subscription record at purchase: amount, currency, interval, plan, trial terms, and the disclosure-copy version — immutable once written.
Version pricing_plans (history table or append-only revisions) so a past price is reconstructable.
Record the billing interval on flipdesk_subscription_events.
Make cancellation_reason append-only per-event rather than a single mutable text column overwritten on each cancel.
Follow the migrations skill: idempotent SQL, EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION bump in the same commit, self-record footer.

The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. The binding obligations today are (a) ROSCA 15 U.S.C. 8403 and FTC Act Section 5, both actively enforced, and (b) STATE automatic-renewal laws — most importantly California's ARL as amended by AB 2863, effective 2025-07-01, which is stricter than what we do today and expressly covers free trials. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). This is the evidentiary half of the consent story — consent to WHAT is unanswerable without it. Also unblocks honest revenue reporting. | 2026-07-19 ALL FOUR SCHEMA ACs DONE (migration 00486) + the write path. ⚠ I FIRST ASSERTED THIS WHOLE COMPLIANCE BATCH WAS GATED ON US-2114 (counsel) AND THAT WAS WRONG — recording it because the error was mine and would have left a P0 sitting untouched. US-2114 gates what the disclosure copy SAYS; this story is about whether we can still PROVE what it said. Those are different questions, and only the first needs a lawyer. Testing the assertion instead of repeating it is what surfaced the work. AC1 subscription_agreements — immutable snapshot at purchase (plan, interval, amount, currency, trial terms, disclosure_version pointer). IMMUTABILITY IS TRIGGER-ENFORCED, not merely intended: UPDATE and DELETE both RAISE. A comment asking people not to edit a compliance record is not a control, and this table's entire value is that its contents cannot drift. disclosure_version is nullable because the copy versioning (US-2114/US-2115) has not landed — recording the POINTER now means no second migration later. AC2 pricing_plan_revisions — append-only history written BY TRIGGER on pricing_plans, deliberately not by the application: a history table that depends on the writer remembering is a history table with gaps. Stores a full jsonb row snapshot too, so a column added to pricing_plans later is captured historically without another migration here. Seeded with current rows as revision zero so the history has a floor rather than implying prices did not exist before today. AC3 flipdesk_subscription_events.billing_interval — the gap 00215's OWN comment recorded; from_plan/to_plan alone cannot distinguish a monthly→yearly switch from a no-op. AC4 subscription_cancellations — append-only; users.cancellation_reason was a single mutable column each cancel overwrote, so a repeat canceller left one reason and no trace it happened twice. Backfilled from that column (timestamped updated_at, the best available approximation — the true cancel time was never recorded, which IS the defect) and the old column is KEPT since readers still use it. WRITE PATH: lib/agreed-terms.ts, pure extraction + a thin IO half, wired into handleSubscriptionChange — chosen over checkout.session because the subscription object carries what Stripe ACTUALLY applied (amount, interval, trial) whereas checkout carries what was requested. THE DESIGN POINT WORTH REVIEWING: it DECLINES TO WRITE rather than writing a partial row when the subscription cannot support a truthful record (no price, no unit_amount, or an interval we do not sell — Stripe also emits day/week). A compliance record containing a plausible guess is worse than a visible gap, because it will be read as fact. The refusal is reported, so the gap is not silent. Best-effort throughout: a compliance record must never be why a paying customer fails to get entitlement. Idempotent via a unique index, so a webhook redelivery cannot mint a second agreement for one purchase. 9 tests. The one that matters most: a MISSING amount must yield NO record while a REAL zero is kept — 0 is a legitimate agreed price (comped/fully-discounted), so defaulting absence to 0 would be indistinguishable from a genuine free agreement on the record. Negative-verified by making absence default to 0; that test goes red. ⚠ THE RLS GUARD CAUGHT MY OWN TABLES, which is the system working: three new tables with owner columns, RLS enabled and no policies is exactly the case US-2008's widened guard exists to catch, and the full suite went red until I classified them. All three are now in SERVICE_ROLE_ONLY with the reasoning — they are evidentiary, read only by admin/support tooling, and the failure mode of a permissive policy (a user reading, or influencing, the record of what they agreed to) is precisely what they exist to rule out. STILL OPEN: nothing schema-side. What remains is US-2114's counsel review before any disclosure COPY ships, and wiring disclosure_version once that copy is versioned. Migration 00486 is HELD (7th) — see PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md for the two backfills and the deploy-order note. | 2026-07-19 ⚠ STALE HELD-MIGRATION CLAIM — do not act on it. The migration(s) this note calls HELD (00215, 00486) are all on origin/main, verified individually with git log origin/main against each file rather than inferred from the linter's summary. The standing rule makes this decisive: a commit containing a migration is NOT pushed until the operator has applied the SQL, so a migration present on origin/main was pushed, which means its hold was already released. PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md agrees — every entry through 00490 (the highest migration in the tree) is marked APPLIED and confirmed by the user, so nothing is genuinely pending. WHY THIS MATTERS ENOUGH TO CORRECT: a stale hold tells the next reader the branch is frozen when it is not, which either invites a pointless prod session or — worse — makes them hold back an unrelated push that was always safe. Correction APPENDED rather than edited into the original sentence, because these notes are append-only and the history of what was believed when is itself worth keeping.

userStories.title: In-place plan upgrade charges a prorated amount on a single click with no confirmation
userStories.description: services/edge-functions/src/routes/payments.ts:326-380: if a user already has a subscription, clicking a higher tier calls stripe.subscriptions.update with proration_behavior: 'create_prorations' — charging immediately with NO Stripe Checkout page, no price confirmation, no interstitial and no disclosure. The click IS the purchase. Every other purchase path at least passes through Stripe's hosted checkout, which renders the recurring price; this one renders nothing.
acceptanceCriteria: Show an explicit confirmation step before an in-place upgrade that states the prorated amount charged today, the new recurring amount, the new billing frequency, and the next renewal date.
Capture the same affirmative consent artifact as a new subscription.
Apply the same treatment to downgrades and interval switches if they charge or change terms.
Test asserting the upgrade mutation cannot fire without the confirmation step.

The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). A charge with no disclosure and no confirmation is the clearest Section 5 / ROSCA exposure in the codebase after the missing disclosures themselves. | 2026-07-19 SCOPED, DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT — and the reason is the story's own logic, not capacity. AC1 needs a confirmation stating the PRORATED AMOUNT CHARGED TODAY, the new recurring amount, the new frequency and the next renewal date. Those numbers do not exist anywhere yet: payments.ts has fetchUpcomingInvoice (US-400) but that returns the CURRENT subscription's upcoming invoice, not a simulation of what a CHANGE would cost. Getting the real figure needs Stripe's proration preview — invoices.retrieveUpcoming with the PROPOSED subscription_items plus a subscription_proration_date — which is a new endpoint, and one whose output I cannot verify from this sandbox (the Stripe MCP connector is unauthorized; see US-2033, blocked the same way). WHY THAT BLOCKS RATHER THAN MERELY SLOWS: a confirmation dialog that states a WRONG prorated amount is worse than the current no-dialog state. Today the defect is an OMISSION — the click is the purchase and nothing is stated. A dialog showing an unverified number converts that into an AFFIRMATIVE MISSTATEMENT about a charge, on the exact surface this compliance batch exists to fix. That is the same reasoning applied in US-2117 (refuse to write a partial agreement), US-2119 (refuse to send a notice with no date) and US-2116 (refuse to record a client-supplied IP): on an evidentiary or money surface, a plausible-looking wrong value is worse than an acknowledged gap. WHAT THE NEXT PASS NEEDS, so it is short: (1) a preview endpoint wrapping invoices.retrieveUpcoming with the target plan's price id, returning prorated-now / new-recurring / interval / next-renewal; (2) a confirmation dialog — DowngradePreviewDialog is the established pattern to mirror, and AC3's 'apply the same treatment to downgrades' is already satisfied by it, which is why upgrades being bare is the anomaly rather than the norm; (3) route the upgrade mutation through it; (4) AC4's test that the mutation cannot fire without confirmation. AC2 (capture the same consent artifact as a new subscription) is now CHEAP because US-2117 landed: subscription_agreements + recordAgreedTerms already exist, and an in-place upgrade produces a customer.subscription.updated event that already flows through handleSubscriptionChange — which now calls recordAgreedTerms. So an upgrade ALREADY writes an agreement row with the new plan/interval/amount. Worth verifying rather than assuming, but the plumbing is in place. The FIGURES are the blocker, and they need a Stripe session — not more code reading. | 2026-07-23 CODE COMPLETE (branch claude/session-planning-jokq5h); edge unvalidated in-sandbox (no deno), CI + a real Stripe test env confirm. The in-place upgrade (payments.ts /flipdesk/subscribe, existing paid sub → higher tier) called stripe.subscriptions.update with create_prorations on a single click — no disclosure, no consent. AC1: new POST /flipdesk/upgrade-preview computes the real proration via stripe.invoices.retrieveUpcoming (simulating the item swap with subscription_items + subscription_proration_behavior) and returns amount_due_today_cents, currency, new_recurring_cents, interval, next_renewal_at (current_period_end). AC4 (server-enforced, the strong guarantee): the in-place path now refuses unless the body carries confirmUpgrade:true — returns 409 { code:'UPGRADE_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED', requiresConfirmation:true } and does NOT mutate; the gate sits BEFORE subscriptions.update. AC2: on a confirmed change it writes a consent artifact to flipdesk_subscription_events (event_type 'in_place_change_confirmed', from/to plan, raw_payload with prices+interval+source) — the equivalent of Checkout's disclosure. Web: new UpgradePreviewDialog (mirrors the existing DowngradePreviewDialog) fetches the preview and discloses amount today / new recurring rate+frequency / next renewal before confirming; the plan picker's upgrade CTA opens it for a paid→higher change and calls subscribe with confirmUpgrade:true on confirm. A free→paid upgrade still goes straight to Stripe Checkout (which discloses on its own hosted page), so it skips the dialog. AC3: downgrades already route through DowngradePreviewDialog and interval switches through the Stripe billing portal (both disclose/confirm) — the upgrade path was the only gap, now closed. TESTS: edge upgrade-confirmation-gate_test.ts asserts (source-structural, this repo's idiom for Stripe-heavy routes — cf. subscription-ack-disclosure_test.ts) that the confirmUpgrade gate precedes the mutation, the preview endpoint + retrieveUpcoming exist, and the consent artifact is written; all 10 assertions verified green by replicating them in node against payments.ts. Verified in-sandbox: web tsc -b + eslint clean; billing+hooks vitest 36/36 green; only flipdesk-plan-picker-dialog uses useFlipdeskSubscribe and only use-billing-summary calls the endpoint, so no other caller now 409s. KEPT passes:false: the edge route + the Stripe preview call are not runnable here (no deno, no Stripe test key); run the deno lane + exercise a real paid→higher upgrade against Stripe test mode to confirm the prorated amount + consent row, then flip.

userStories.title: No advance renewal reminder exists anywhere — annual plans are charged silently
userStories.description: Confirmed absence, verified three ways: invoice.upcoming is NOT in the Stripe webhook switch (services/edge-functions/src/routes/webhooks.ts:244-281, falls through to a default log-and-drop at :281); no cron in jobs-cron-fleet.ts sends one; and the only upcoming_invoice reference is a read-only pull for the billing page (payments.ts:1142). The first notice a user receives about a renewal is sendSubscriptionRenewalReceiptEmail (email.ts:1183), sent AFTER the money is taken. Yearly price IDs exist for all five paid tiers (src/lib/constants.ts:1344-1366) and flow through the identical path — interval only changes a display string — so an annual subscriber is charged a full year's fee with no prior contact whatsoever.
acceptanceCriteria: Handle invoice.upcoming and send a transactional advance renewal notice stating the amount, the date of the charge, the plan, and how to cancel before it.
Configure the Stripe lead time explicitly rather than relying on the default, and set a longer lead for annual plans than monthly.
Send via deliverEmail as a TRANSACTIONAL category — it must not be routed through the drip/marketing engine where opt-out, suppression or frequency caps can silently drop it.
Also handle customer.subscription.trial_will_end.
Test that an annual subscription produces a reminder before renewal and that a marketing opt-out does not suppress it.

Advance notice before a long-term renewal is a common state-ARL requirement and we have annual plans in production. Cheapest structural fix in the batch: one webhook case reusing existing email infrastructure. | 2026-07-19 AC1 + AC3 + AC4 + AC5 DONE (mechanism, not copy — the fourth compliance story that did not need counsel). invoice.upcoming is now HANDLED and sends sendRenewalReminderEmail, a NEW template deliberately separate from sendSubscriptionRenewalReceiptEmail: a receipt confirms something that happened, this warns about something that has not, and the only action that matters — cancel before the date — is meaningless on a receipt. It states the plan, the amount, the exact charge date and how to cancel. AC3: category subscription_renewal_reminder is registered in TRANSACTIONAL_CATEGORIES, so resolveIsMarketing force-classifies it transactional even if marketing:true is explicitly requested — pinned by a test, because if that ever flips, an opt-out silently drops the only advance warning of a charge and the exact defect returns. AC4 customer.subscription.trial_will_end is handled too, and THE DISJOINTNESS IS THE INTERESTING PART: our signup trial has NO Stripe subscription (handle_new_user grants it directly), and US-2120's cron filters flipdesk_subscription_id IS NULL. This event fires only for a STRIPE-managed trial — someone who started a PAID subscription with a trial period — which is exactly the user that cron skips. The two populations cannot overlap, so neither path double-sends. A test asserts the cron keeps that filter, since removing it would make both fire for the same person. It reuses sendTrialExpiringEmail rather than minting a second trial template, because two near-identical trial emails drift. DECLINES TO SEND WITHOUT A DATE: if Stripe supplies neither next_payment_attempt nor period_end the handler returns. A notice that cannot say WHEN is not a notice, and 'you will be charged at some point' is worse than silence. Same reasoning as US-2117's refusal to write a partial agreement. TWO OF MY OWN EARLIER ARTEFACTS CAUGHT THIS CHANGE, which is the guards working: (1) the US-2128 test asserting invoice.upcoming and trial_will_end were on the known-ignored list went RED, correctly — they had graduated to real handlers, and a handled event must never ALSO be listed as ignored or the list is lying. userStories.title: Trial-ending notice is a suppressible marketing drip, not a transactional notice
userStories.description: sendTrialExpiringEmail (email.ts:1391) is well-written, states the end date, and is DEAD CODE — its only reference outside its own definition is a test (src/tests/email-category_test.ts:25). It was deliberately decommissioned (routes/notifications.ts:830) in favour of the US-943 drip engine. What replaced it is unambiguously marketing: it ships via sendDripStepEmail (email.ts:2570) with a one-click marketing unsubscribe footer, and routes/drip.ts:526-574 skips the send entirely when optedOut || suppressed || frequencyCapped. So a user who unsubscribes from marketing receives NO trial-ending notice at all. The seed copy (00255_drip_campaign_definitions.sql:134-135) states neither a charge amount nor a charge date, carries an {{incentive}} coupon block, and is operator-editable at runtime with no guaranteed terms.
acceptanceCriteria: Restore a transactional trial-ending notice that cannot be suppressed by marketing opt-out, suppression lists or frequency caps — sendTrialExpiringEmail already exists and needs a caller.
It must state what happens at trial end: whether a charge occurs, the amount and date if so, and how to cancel or avoid it.
Keep the marketing drip for conversion messaging, but the required notice must not depend on it.
Test that a marketing-opted-out trialist still receives the transactional notice.

The email was never the problem; the absence of a caller was. AC3 satisfied by construction: the marketing drip is untouched, so conversion messaging continues — what changed is that the REQUIRED notice no longer depends on it. AC2 IS FACTUALLY SATISFIABLE WITHOUT COUNSEL, and I verified the fact rather than assuming: jobs-trial-expiry sets flipdesk_plan='free', subscription_status='none' — the trial LAPSES, it does not charge. Pinned by a test. ⚠ ONE HONEST LIMITATION, stated rather than hidden: dedupe is the exact-day window (daysLeft === 3), not a stored marker. Third time this session a guard matched my prose rather than code; anchored on sendDripStepEmail( with the paren. Verified: edge 4301 passed, deno check + lint clean. | 2026-07-19 VERIFIED ALREADY DONE (stale story). The premise — 'sendTrialExpiringEmail is DEAD CODE, its only reference is a test' — is no longer true: routes/jobs-trial-expiry.ts imports and calls it (:21, :122) as a transactional send, and webhooks.ts reuses it for the Stripe-managed trial path rather than minting a marketing variant (:2181). NOT flipping passes myself — AC4 asks for a test proving a marketing-opted-out trialist still receives it, and I did not confirm such a test exists. | 2026-07-22 CLOSED (verification, no code change needed). acceptanceCriteria: Disclose the trial on the signup screen: that one is being started, its length, that no card is required, and what happens at the end (features drop to Free — no charge).

userStories.title: Post-purchase acknowledgement omits the auto-renewal statement and how to cancel
